learningObjectives: Identify threshold, depolarisation, repolarisation and after-hyperpolarisation.
Explain sodium-channel activation and inactivation.
Distinguish absolute from relative refractory periods.
Relate firing patterns to neural coding and clinical excitability.

anatomy.label: Threshold
anatomy.detail: Threshold is the membrane voltage at which inward sodium current becomes self-amplifying and an action potential is initiated.
anatomy.clinical: Threshold is dynamic and shifts with recent activity, neuromodulation and channel state.

anatomy.label: Voltage-gated sodium channels
anatomy.detail: Sodium channels open quickly with depolarisation, then inactivate even while the membrane remains depolarised.
anatomy.clinical: Sodium-channel blockers can reduce pathological high-frequency firing.

anatomy.label: Voltage-gated potassium channels
anatomy.detail: Potassium channels open more slowly, allowing potassium efflux that returns voltage toward baseline.
anatomy.clinical: Altered potassium conductance can prolong spikes or destabilise firing.

anatomy.label: Refractory periods
anatomy.detail: During the absolute refractory period most sodium channels are inactivated; during the relative period stronger input may still trigger firing.
anatomy.clinical: Refractoriness limits firing rate and helps action potentials travel in one direction.

interaction.instruction: Select a component, then run the sequence to see how the system changes over time.

stages.label: Threshold
stages.text: Summed input depolarises the axon initial segment to threshold.

stages.label: Upstroke
stages.text: Voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium enters rapidly.

stages.label: Repolarise
stages.text: Sodium channels inactivate while potassium channels open.

stages.label: Recover
stages.text: After-hyperpolarisation and channel recovery restore readiness.

quizBank.question: What directly produces the rapid upstroke of an action potential?
quizBank.explanation: Rapid sodium influx drives the depolarising upstroke.

quizBank.question: Why does an action potential not normally travel backward?
quizBank.explanation: The refractory region behind the spike cannot immediately regenerate another action potential.

quizBank.question: What ends the sodium current during the spike?
quizBank.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels rapidly enter an inactivated state.

quizBank.question: During the relative refractory period:
options: A stronger-than-usual input may trigger another spike
No spike is possible under any condition
The neuron has no membrane voltage
All potassium channels are permanently closed
quizBank.explanation: Residual potassium conductance means stronger depolarisation is needed.

quizBank.question: Action-potential amplitude usually encodes stimulus strength by:
options: It generally does not; rate and timing carry more information
Growing larger with every stronger stimulus
quizBank.explanation: Individual spikes are stereotyped; firing pattern conveys intensity and context.

sections.explainSimply: Acute stress prepares the body to act through fast autonomic and hormonal responses.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Attention narrows, salience rises, memory encoding changes and flexible reasoning may temporarily reduce as survival priorities dominate.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Catecholamines act rapidly; HPA-axis cortisol follows more slowly. Response magnitude depends on predictability, controllability, prior learning and current safety.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of acute stress response as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need acute stress response to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A strong acute response can be adaptive and is not itself a disorder.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use acute stress response to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses acute stress response to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: A strong acute response can be adaptive and is not itself a disorder. Evidence classification: established physiology.

adhd-neurofeedback.title: ADHD Applications

sections.explainSimply: Neurofeedback has been studied as a training approach for ADHD symptoms, especially attention and self-regulation.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Earlier meta-analyses reported benefits, but rigorous blinded outcomes and recent syntheses have produced less favourable conclusions at group level.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Discuss evidence uncertainty, standard treatments, burden, cost and the difference between proximal ratings and blinded outcomes. Do not replace indicated care without shared decision-making.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Testing a treatment hypothesis: improvement must be meaningful, measured and compared with plausible alternatives.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand adhd applications to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A child improving during a long treatment course does not prove neurofeedback caused the change.
sections.clinicalPearl: Measure benefit and harm with the same seriousness.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using adhd applications predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: A child improving during a long treatment course does not prove neurofeedback caused the change. Evidence classification: mixed; recent high-quality synthesis does not show meaningful group-level benefit.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the core clinical distinction?
reviewPrompts.answer: Name the feared catastrophe, not just the symptom. “Anxiety” is the alarm; the formulation is the prediction.

Amygdala-centred accounts are insufficient. Anxiety reflects interactions among insula, anterior cingulate, hippocampus, prefrontal regulation, periaqueductal grey, autonomic systems and learning history. Avoidance prevents prediction error and maintains overestimation of danger. Effective exposure is inhibitory learning: building new safety or tolerability associations rather than erasing fear.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What red flags or alternatives matter?
reviewPrompts.answer: Acute chest pain, syncope, neurological deficits, intoxication, withdrawal or endocrine disturbance can mimic anxiety and require medical consideration. Trauma, autism-related overload and psychosis also demand differential assessment.

sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Location: Arterial territories cover cortical surfaces, deep nuclei, white matter, brainstem and cerebellum with substantial anatomical variation and collateral overlap. Major subdivisions include anterior cerebral artery territory, middle cerebral artery territory, posterior cerebral artery territory, lenticulostriate arteries, anterior choroidal artery, posterior inferior cerebellar artery, anterior inferior cerebellar artery, superior cerebellar artery, basilar perforators. Inputs include internal carotid circulation, vertebrobasilar circulation, circle of Willis collateral routes; outputs include cortical branches, deep perforators, brainstem and cerebellar branches.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A dynamic transport and control map: the meaning of any node depends on the routes entering, leaving and bypassing it.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Post-stroke mood, fatigue, apathy and cognitive change reflect lesion location, network disconnection, systemic illness, disability and psychosocial context rather than a single “stroke personality.”

anatomy.label: Astrocyte soma
anatomy.detail: The soma contains the nucleus and biosynthetic machinery that maintain the astrocyte's extensive territorial processes. A single astrocyte can coordinate local homeostasis across many synapses.
anatomy.clinical: Astrocytes are metabolically active cells, not inert packing material. Their failure can alter neuronal function even when neurons remain structurally intact.

anatomy.label: Perisynaptic processes
anatomy.detail: Very fine astrocytic processes approach or envelop synapses. They sense transmitter release, shape extracellular chemistry and help limit spillover between neighbouring synapses.
anatomy.clinical: The tripartite synapse frames transmission as an interaction among the presynaptic neuron, postsynaptic neuron and nearby astrocyte.

anatomy.label: Glutamate transporters
anatomy.detail: Astrocytic excitatory amino-acid transporters, especially EAAT2 in humans, remove much of the glutamate released into the extracellular space. Astrocytes then convert glutamate to glutamine for reuse by neurons.
anatomy.clinical: Impaired glutamate clearance can increase excitotoxic stress and destabilise networks. This is clinically relevant to epilepsy, injury and several neurodegenerative conditions.

anatomy.label: Potassium buffering
anatomy.detail: Neuronal firing raises extracellular potassium. Astrocytes take up and redistribute potassium through channels and coupled networks, helping preserve the gradients required for reliable excitability.
anatomy.clinical: Failure of potassium homeostasis can lower seizure threshold and amplify pathological synchrony.

anatomy.label: Vascular endfeet
anatomy.detail: Astrocytic endfeet closely cover cerebral microvessels. They participate in the neurovascular unit, support barrier properties and help match local perfusion to neural activity.
anatomy.clinical: Functional imaging relies on neurovascular coupling. BOLD signal is therefore an indirect haemodynamic correlate of neural activity, shaped by neuron–glia–vascular interactions.

anatomy.label: Metabolic support
anatomy.detail: Astrocytes store glycogen, process glucose and provide metabolic substrates that support active neurons. Their position between synapses and blood vessels makes them key coordinators of local energy demand.
anatomy.clinical: Sleep loss, hypoxia and metabolic stress can impair cognition partly by disturbing the systems that support neuronal energy use.

anatomy.label: Gap-junction network
anatomy.detail: Astrocytes connect to neighbouring astrocytes through gap junctions, allowing ions and small molecules to redistribute across a functional network rather than remaining confined to one cell.
anatomy.clinical: Homeostasis is distributed. A local disturbance may be buffered across an astrocytic network, but widespread dysfunction can reduce that reserve.

A microglial nucleus in the postsynaptic neuron
quizBank.explanation: The tripartite concept recognises the perisynaptic astrocyte as an active participant alongside pre- and postsynaptic neuronal elements.

quizBank.question: Why is astrocytic potassium buffering important?
options: It stabilises neuronal excitability after firing
It generates action potentials in myelin
It creates cerebrospinal fluid in ventricles
quizBank.explanation: Neuronal activity raises extracellular potassium; astrocytes help redistribute it so membrane gradients and network stability are maintained.

quizBank.question: Astrocytic vascular endfeet are part of which functional system?
quizBank.explanation: Endfeet contact cerebral microvessels and contribute to barrier support, metabolic exchange and activity-linked blood-flow regulation.

quizBank.question: Which statement about reactive astrogliosis is most accurate?
options: It can be protective or maladaptive depending on context and duration
It always means astrocytes have died
It is identical to bacterial meningitis
It has no effect on neuronal networks
quizBank.explanation: Reactive astrocyte responses are heterogeneous. They may contain injury and restore homeostasis, but persistent or dysregulated responses can also impede recovery.

anatomy.label: Ventral attention network
anatomy.detail: Right-lateralised temporoparietal and ventral frontal regions respond to unexpected, relevant events.
anatomy.clinical: Disruption can contribute to spatial neglect and impaired reorienting.

anatomy.label: Alerting systems

anatomy.label: Executive attention

mechanismMap.label: Core function
mechanismMap.detail: Attention is the brain’s way of choosing what gets priority. It helps you notice what matters, stay with it, ignore distractions and switch when the task changes.

mechanismMap.label: Neural systems
mechanismMap.detail: Attention emerges from interacting dorsal and ventral attention systems, thalamic and brainstem arousal mechanisms, frontoparietal control networks and neuromodulatory systems. Test scores are highly state-sensitive: sleep, pain, anxiety, medication, effort and task novelty can alter performance without indicating a fixed attentional deficit.

mechanismMap.label: Assessment pattern
mechanismMap.detail: Attention is not one unitary skill. Clinical assessment distinguishes alertness, sustained attention, selective attention, divided attention and attentional control. Performance depends on arousal, motivation, sensory load, working memory and executive regulation.

mechanismMap.label: Clinical translation
mechanismMap.detail: Psychologists need to separate trait-like attentional vulnerability from situational overload, slowed processing, mood-related interference and executive dyscontrol. This distinction changes both diagnosis and intervention.

sections.explainSimply: Some autistic people use neurofeedback with goals such as attention, sleep or self-regulation.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Autism is not a unitary brain-wave abnormality. Goals should be person-centred and avoid framing neurodivergence itself as damage to be normalised.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: A 2025 systematic review found signals of cognitive benefit across a small, heterogeneous literature, but the evidence base remains too limited and methodologically variable to infer efficacy for autism as a condition. Define person-centred functional targets, monitor sensory load and assent, and avoid normalisation goals.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Testing a treatment hypothesis: improvement must be meaningful, measured and compared with plausible alternatives.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand autism applications to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not promise to “treat autism” or erase identity-linked traits.
sections.clinicalPearl: Measure benefit and harm with the same seriousness.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using autism applications predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not promise to “treat autism” or erase identity-linked traits. Evidence classification: preliminary and heterogeneous; selected cognitive outcomes are not evidence that autism itself is normalised or cured.

anatomy.label: Hypothalamus
anatomy.detail: Hypothalamic nuclei organise temperature, energy, fluid and defensive responses.

anatomy.label: Brainstem autonomic nuclei
anatomy.detail: NTS and medullary networks integrate visceral afferents and regulate output.

anatomy.label: Parasympathetic pathways
anatomy.detail: Craniosacral output, especially vagal pathways, regulates heart, lungs and gut.
anatomy.clinical: Vagal effects are organ-specific; “more vagal” is not universally better.

sections.explainSimply: Trace direct, indirect and hyperdirect loops through cortex, striatum, pallidum, subthalamic nucleus and thalamus.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Frontostriatal loops influence motivation, reinforcement learning, response inhibition and cognitive flexibility; abnormalities are transdiagnostic rather than disorder-specific.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Location: Deep bilateral nuclei surrounding the internal capsule, linked with frontal cortex, thalamus and midbrain. Major subdivisions include caudate nucleus, putamen, nucleus accumbens, globus pallidus external, globus pallidus internal, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra pars compacta, substantia nigra pars reticulata, motor thalamus. Inputs include frontal cortex, sensorimotor cortex, limbic cortex, substantia nigra pars compacta; outputs include motor thalamus, brainstem motor regions, frontal cortex via thalamus.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A dynamic transport and control map: the meaning of any node depends on the routes entering, leaving and bypassing it.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Frontostriatal loops influence motivation, reinforcement learning, response inhibition and cognitive flexibility; abnormalities are transdiagnostic rather than disorder-specific.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Disruption may contribute to hypokinetic or hyperkinetic movement, impaired initiation, altered habit learning, impulsivity or apathy. Clinical expression depends on circuit, laterality, cause and network compensation.
sections.clinicalPearl: Do not reduce the basal ganglia to “movement centres”: specify the motor, associative or limbic loop and the direction of circuit imbalance.
sections.practicalExample: Select a region, trace its incoming and outgoing pathways, then compare healthy and lesion overlays before forming a clinical hypothesis.
sections.limitationsCautions: Circuit diagrams are simplified. Neurotransmitters, receptor subtypes, oscillatory state and disease stage can reverse or modify net effects. Anatomy cannot diagnose a psychiatric disorder.

anatomy.position: Deep bilateral nuclei surrounding the internal capsule, linked with frontal cortex, thalamus and midbrain.
anatomy.spatialRelationships: Interpreted relative to connected cortical, subcortical and vascular structures; boundaries and laterality must be checked in the selected view.
anatomy.bloodSupply: Primarily perforating branches of the middle and anterior cerebral arteries, including lenticulostriate and recurrent artery of Heubner territories; vascular anatomy varies.
anatomy.lesionEffects: Disruption may contribute to hypokinetic or hyperkinetic movement, impaired initiation, altered habit learning, impulsivity or apathy. Clinical expression depends on circuit, laterality, cause and network compensation.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Frontostriatal loops influence motivation, reinforcement learning, response inhibition and cognitive flexibility; abnormalities are transdiagnostic rather than disorder-specific.

quiz.question: Which pathway provides a rapid cortical route to increase inhibitory basal-ganglia output?
quiz.rationale: The hyperdirect pathway projects from cortex to subthalamic nucleus, rapidly increasing GPi/SNr output and suppressing competing actions.

quiz.question: Dopamine from substantia nigra pars compacta generally has what net effect on movement-related striatal circuitry?
options: Facilitates selected actions through D1 and D2 receptor effects
Has no effect on action selection
quiz.rationale: Dopamine tends to facilitate selected actions by exciting D1 direct-pathway neurons and reducing D2 indirect-pathway influence, although real circuitry is more complex.

quiz.question: What is the safest interpretation of apathy in relation to basal-ganglia circuits?
options: It may reflect frontostriatal network dysfunction but is nonspecific
quiz.rationale: Apathy can arise from several frontal-subcortical, medical and psychiatric processes and requires broader assessment.

pathways.label: Direct pathway
pathways.summary: Facilitates selected motor programmes by reducing inhibitory basal-ganglia output to thalamocortical systems.
pathways.healthy: Cortical activation of striatal direct-pathway neurons suppresses GPi output, disinhibiting motor thalamus and supporting the selected action.
pathways.disrupted: Reduced effective direct-pathway facilitation can contribute to hypokinesia and impaired movement initiation, but clinical syndromes reflect the balance of multiple loops rather than one pathway in isolation.

pathways.label: Indirect pathway
pathways.summary: Suppresses competing actions through striatal, pallidal and subthalamic interactions.
pathways.healthy: The indirect pathway helps constrain competing motor programmes by increasing effective inhibitory output from GPi.
pathways.disrupted: Loss of subthalamic drive can reduce GPi inhibition of thalamus and contribute to hyperkinetic movement, classically contralateral ballistic movements with focal STN injury.

pathways.label: Nigrostriatal modulation
pathways.summary: Dopamine from substantia nigra pars compacta modulates striatal activity and shifts the balance of direct and indirect pathways.
pathways.healthy: Nigrostriatal dopamine modulates multiple striatal cell populations to support flexible scaling and initiation of action.
pathways.disrupted: Progressive nigrostriatal dopamine loss contributes to bradykinesia, rigidity and other Parkinsonian features, while the full disorder involves broader circuits and non-dopaminergic systems.

cases.label: Case 1
cases.prompt: After a small unilateral deep lesion, a patient develops abrupt, large-amplitude flinging movements of the contralateral limbs.
cases.rationale: Focal subthalamic nucleus injury is classically associated with contralateral hemiballismus through reduced excitatory drive to basal-ganglia output nuclei.
cases.caveat: Other lesions and metabolic causes can produce chorea or ballistic movements; the clinical pattern must be confirmed with examination and imaging.

comparisons.label: Direct pathway balance

healthy.label: Adaptive action facilitation
healthy.summary: Direct and indirect pathway activity is balanced to facilitate selected actions while suppressing competitors.
healthy.mechanism: Striatal, pallidal, subthalamic, nigral and thalamic nodes regulate thalamo-cortical output.
healthy.observable: Movement initiation and behavioural selection are appropriately scaled to context.

pathology.label: Reduced facilitation / excessive inhibition
pathology.summary: Disrupted circuit balance can reduce effective thalamo-cortical drive.
pathology.mechanism: Changes in dopaminergic modulation or basal-ganglia output alter action gating.
pathology.observable: Bradykinetic or initiation-related difficulties may occur, depending on cause and circuit involvement.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: Basal-ganglia effects extend beyond pure movement because parallel loops contribute to cognitive and motivational selection.
comparisons.assessment: Consider motor findings, initiation, processing speed, executive control, medication state and neurological diagnosis together.
comparisons.caveat: The classic direct/indirect model is a useful teaching simplification, not a complete account of basal-ganglia physiology.

comparisons.label: Dopaminergic modulation

healthy.label: Modulated striatal gating
healthy.summary: Nigrostriatal dopamine helps tune activity across striatal receptor populations and action-selection circuits.
healthy.mechanism: Dopaminergic input changes excitability and plasticity within cortico-basal-ganglia loops.
healthy.observable: Action initiation and reinforcement-related learning are modulated flexibly.

pathology.label: Reduced nigrostriatal modulation
pathology.summary: Loss or dysfunction of dopaminergic input changes the balance of basal-ganglia output.
pathology.mechanism: Altered striatal modulation affects downstream pallidal and thalamic influence on cortex.
pathology.observable: Motor slowing and changes in learning or motivation may occur depending on disease and stage.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: Avoid reducing complex behaviour to “low dopamine”; dopamine acts in multiple circuits and clinical phenotype depends on the broader system.
comparisons.assessment: Interpret cognition and behaviour alongside motor state, medication timing, disease stage and mood.
comparisons.caveat: Dopamine is neither globally high nor low in a simple way across disorders, receptors, regions or time.

assessmentLab.title: Assessment-linked basal ganglia reasoning
assessmentLab.instruction: Use observed behaviour and targeted tasks to test a circuit hypothesis rather than inferring a diagnosis from one motor or cognitive feature.

cases.label: Motor initiation
cases.prompt: A patient is slow to initiate actions and appears effortful despite preserved basic strength. What is the most informative first functional domain?
cases.rationale: Basal ganglia circuit dysfunction often affects initiation, movement scaling and speed; the pattern should be separated from weakness, comprehension problems and low effort.
taskTypes: executive speed tasks with motor demands interpreted cautiously
supports: consistent bradykinetic or initiation pattern across tasks
motor slowing disproportionate to comprehension demands
challenges: isolated cognitive slowing without motor features
primary weakness or pain limiting movement
performance varying mainly with anxiety or task novelty
cases.nextStep: Integrate neurological examination, medication effects and functional history before attributing the pattern to a basal ganglia circuit.
cases.caveat: Processing speed measures are multiply determined; motor, visual, attentional and motivational demands must be separated.

cases.label: Reward / control circuit
cases.prompt: A patient shows marked reward-driven choices and poor delay tolerance. Which assessment domain best tests the circuit-level hypothesis?
cases.rationale: Frontostriatal reward-control hypotheses require evidence about reinforcement sensitivity, inhibition and decision-making across contexts, not a single impulsive act.
observe: effect of fatigue, mood, substances and medication
supports: cross-context disinhibition linked to reward salience
challenges: behaviour confined to one interpersonal context
intact inhibitory control across structured tasks and everyday settings
better explanation by acute mood, substance or environmental factors
cases.nextStep: Use multiple methods and collateral information; do not equate impulsivity with a specific circuit or disorder.
cases.caveat: Reward and inhibition are distributed network functions and are strongly shaped by development, context and psychiatric state.

brain-lateralisation-comparison.title: Brain Lateralisation Comparison
brain-lateralisation-comparison.subtitle: Compare hemispheric specialisation without reducing people to left-brain or right-brain types
brain-lateralisation-comparison.altText: Chalkboard-style paired cerebral hemispheres linked by the corpus callosum, with language, attention, prosody, motor and visual-field networks shown as overlapping rather than isolated systems.
learningObjectives: Compare common hemispheric asymmetries while recognising bilateral and distributed contributions.
Explain how the corpus callosum and other commissures support interhemispheric coordination.
Relate lesion laterality to qualified hypotheses about aphasia, neglect, prosody, motor and visual-field findings.
Explain why handedness and personality do not determine an individual's cerebral organisation.

sections.explainSimply: The hemispheres work as a connected pair. Some operations are weighted more strongly to one side, but neither hemisphere is a complete personality or a self-sufficient thinking style.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Language is commonly left-lateralised, whereas right-lateralised networks often contribute strongly to broad spatial attention, emotional prosody and discourse context. These are population tendencies within bilateral systems, not personality categories or stand-alone diagnostic markers.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Hemispheric specialisation emerges from asymmetries in cortical organisation, intrahemispheric connectivity and interhemispheric coordination. In most right-handers and many left-handers, core language production and comprehension are left-weighted, although bilateral and right-dominant patterns occur. Right frontoparietal attention systems show an important asymmetry: right-sided networks attend broadly across space, while left-sided attention is more strongly biased contralaterally. Lesion effects depend on cortical and subcortical extent, white-matter disconnection, vascular territory, premorbid organisation, diaschisis and recovery.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A skilled two-person team: each member may take the lead for particular operations, but useful performance depends on continuous exchange and shared context.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Laterality helps formulate aphasia, neglect, aprosodia, awareness, memory and executive presentations. It should guide testable hypotheses, not be used to infer creativity, logic, personality or diagnosis from preferences or handedness.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Dominant perisylvian injury may impair language; right frontoparietal injury may produce left neglect or impaired awareness; right perisylvian injury may alter affective prosody; callosal injury may cause task-specific disconnection signs. Real presentations frequently overlap or depart from textbook patterns.
sections.clinicalPearl: Ask which network, pathway and side are affected—and what the person could do before the lesion—rather than asking whether someone is left-brained or right-brained.
sections.practicalExample: Compare a person with fluent but empty speech after a dominant posterior temporal lesion with a person who omits the left side of space after a right frontoparietal lesion, then identify findings that require broader differential diagnosis.
sections.limitationsCautions: Language dominance cannot be inferred reliably from handedness alone. Functional imaging, stimulation and behavioural tests answer different questions, and reorganisation after early injury or epilepsy can alter expected patterns. Group averages do not establish an individual's anatomy.

anatomy.position: Paired cerebral hemispheres separated by the longitudinal fissure and connected by the corpus callosum, anterior and posterior commissures and subcortical pathways.
anatomy.spatialRelationships: Homologous cortical regions face across the midline; each hemisphere receives predominantly contralateral somatosensory and motor information, while visual pathways divide information by visual hemifield rather than by eye.
anatomy.bloodSupply: Lateralised syndromes commonly follow asymmetric ACA, MCA, PCA or deep perforator lesions; vascular boundaries and functional dominance vary between individuals.
anatomy.lesionEffects: Possible findings include aphasia, apraxia of speech, hemispatial neglect, extinction, anosognosia, aprosodia, contralateral weakness or sensory loss, homonymous visual-field loss and callosal disconnection signs. No single finding is explained by hemisphere alone.
psychologicalPresentations: distress and adjustment effects shaped by disability and context
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Laterality narrows hypotheses about affected networks and pathways, but interpretation requires direct assessment, imaging, premorbid context and differential diagnosis.

explorerParts.label: Dominant language network
explorerParts.detail: Inferior frontal, posterior temporal, inferior parietal and connecting dorsal and ventral pathways commonly show left-weighted language organisation.
explorerParts.clinical: Dominant-hemisphere injury may produce different aphasia or speech-motor patterns depending on cortical, subcortical and tract involvement.

explorerParts.label: Right attention network
explorerParts.detail: Right frontal and parietal attention systems contribute to monitoring both sides of space and reorienting toward salient events.
explorerParts.clinical: Right-sided injury more often causes severe and persistent left neglect, but neglect is a network disorder rather than a single-lobe sign.

explorerParts.label: Prosody and discourse
explorerParts.detail: Right-lateralised temporal and frontal contributions help process affective prosody, discourse coherence, humour and contextual inference within bilateral communication systems.
explorerParts.clinical: Right-hemisphere lesions may cause receptive or expressive aprosodia and discourse difficulties, with considerable individual variability.

explorerParts.label: Sensorimotor laterality
explorerParts.detail: Each hemisphere predominantly controls and represents the opposite side of the body, although axial, proximal and some cranial functions receive bilateral influence.
explorerParts.clinical: Lesion level and tract anatomy determine whether weakness, sensory loss, apraxia or other motor-control deficits accompany cortical signs.

explorerParts.label: Visual hemifields
explorerParts.short: Left space to right cortex; right space to left cortex
explorerParts.detail: Post-chiasmal visual pathways route each visual hemifield to the contralateral occipital cortex, combining information from both eyes.
explorerParts.clinical: Retro-chiasmal lesions may cause contralateral homonymous field loss; this differs from attentional neglect, although both can coexist.

explorerParts.label: Corpus callosum
explorerParts.detail: Callosal fibres link homologous and heterologous cortical regions, supporting both cooperative exchange and task-dependent modulation between hemispheres.
explorerParts.clinical: Callosal disconnection can reveal task-specific transfer deficits; it does not create two ordinary independent personalities.

explorerParts.label: Individual variation
explorerParts.detail: Most right-handers and many left-handers show left-weighted language, while bilateral and right-dominant organisation also occur.
explorerParts.clinical: Presurgical and complex neurological decisions require individual functional assessment rather than inference from handedness.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes hemispheric lateralisation?
options: Relative specialisation within strongly connected bilateral systems
Separate logical and creative personality types
Complete independence of the two hemispheres
A fixed trait determined only by handedness
quiz.rationale: Lateralisation describes relative functional weighting; most complex behaviour depends on bilateral networks and interhemispheric exchange.

quiz.question: Why can a right frontoparietal lesion produce severe left hemispatial neglect?
options: Right attention networks contribute broadly to monitoring and reorienting across space
The right hemisphere sees only through the right eye
All spatial processing occurs in one parietal point
Neglect is simply a visual-field defect
quiz.rationale: Right-lateralised attention networks have broad spatial contributions; neglect reflects disrupted attention networks and differs from primary visual-field loss.

quiz.question: What is the safest inference from left-handedness?

brain-overview.title: Meet the Brain
brain-overview.subtitle: One organ, many coordinated systems
learningObjectives: Describe the brain as interacting cortical, subcortical, cerebellar and brainstem systems.
Explain why connectivity is as clinically important as regional specialisation.
Use regional activation cautiously and avoid reverse inference.

sections.explainSimply: The brain is a team of regions that share information. No single area works completely alone.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Functions emerge from distributed networks spanning cortex, subcortex, cerebellum and brainstem. Regional specialisation matters, but connectivity determines performance.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Large-scale networks dynamically reconfigure according to task demands, arousal and learning. Structure–function relationships are probabilistic, not one-to-one mappings.
sections.thinkOfItLike: An orchestra: sections specialise, but the music depends on timing, coordination and the conductor’s changing demands.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Avoid reverse inference—observing activation in a region does not prove a specific thought, diagnosis or emotion.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Focal lesions can disrupt specialised functions, while diffuse or connectivity disturbances may produce broader cognitive and emotional effects.
sections.clinicalPearl: Think in systems first, regions second, and isolated “brain centres” last.
sections.practicalExample: A patient with a focal lesion may show deficits beyond the damaged tissue because connected network nodes lose input or alter their activity. Behaviour therefore reflects both local damage and network consequences.
sections.limitationsCautions: Functional labels are probabilistic summaries. Individual organisation varies with development, experience, pathology and task demands, and neuroimaging activation is not equivalent to a diagnosis.

quizBank.question: Which statement best reflects modern neuroscience?
options: Each emotion has one brain centre
quizBank.explanation: Most psychological functions rely on coordinated activity across distributed, interacting networks.

learningObjectives: Differentiate midbrain, pons and medulla.

sections.explainSimply: The brainstem links the brain, spinal cord and cerebellum while regulating breathing, heart rate, sleep, arousal and many cranial-nerve functions.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Brainstem systems shape state regulation, sensory gating and autonomic stability, meaning small lesions can produce broad cognitive, behavioural and medical effects.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The midbrain, pons and medulla contain cranial-nerve nuclei, reticular formation, long ascending and descending tracts, neuromodulatory nuclei and cardiorespiratory centres. Compact anatomy makes focal lesions clinically dense and often crossed in their signs.
sections.thinkOfItLike: It is a compact transport hub and life-support control room: major routes pass through while local stations regulate essential functions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Changes in arousal, eye movements, swallowing, autonomic regulation or crossed sensory-motor signs can indicate urgent brainstem pathology.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Attributing fluctuating consciousness or cranial-nerve changes to anxiety without neurological assessment may delay recognition of serious disease.
sections.clinicalPearl: Brainstem symptoms are often disproportionate to lesion size because many critical pathways are packed into a small space.
sections.practicalExample: A pontine lesion may combine ipsilateral facial weakness with contralateral limb weakness because a cranial-nerve nucleus and corticospinal tract are affected together.
sections.limitationsCautions: New diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria, collapse, respiratory change or altered consciousness warrants urgent medical assessment.

pathways.label: Long-tract transit
pathways.summary: Descending motor and ascending sensory systems traverse compact brainstem corridors while interacting with cranial-nerve nuclei.
pathways.healthy: Long pathways carry information through successive brainstem levels while local nuclei add cranial, autonomic and cerebellar functions.
pathways.disrupted: A focal brainstem lesion can combine ipsilateral cranial-nerve findings with contralateral long-tract deficits, creating crossed neurological signs.

pathways.label: Ascending arousal system
pathways.summary: Diffuse reticular systems project rostrally to thalamic, hypothalamic and cortical arousal networks.
pathways.healthy: Distributed reticular and ascending projections support wakefulness, attention and state regulation.
pathways.disrupted: Bilateral or strategically placed lesions affecting ascending arousal systems can markedly reduce consciousness, but coma localisation requires full neurological and systemic assessment.

lesionLab.title: Brainstem localisation challenge
lesionLab.instruction: Use the combination of cranial, long-tract and arousal findings to choose the best level or system.

cases.label: Case 1
cases.prompt: A focal syndrome combines an ipsilateral cranial-nerve deficit with contralateral limb weakness and sensory change.
cases.rationale: Crossed signs strongly suggest a brainstem localisation where cranial-nerve structures and ascending or descending long tracts lie in close proximity.
cases.caveat: The exact level depends on which cranial nerve and tract modalities are affected; this simplified map is not sufficient for bedside localisation.

cases.label: Case 2
cases.prompt: Following a central brainstem injury, the dominant change is profound reduction in wakefulness without a simple isolated limb syndrome.
cases.rationale: The reticular formation and associated ascending arousal systems are central to wakefulness and state regulation.
cases.caveat: Reduced consciousness has many structural, metabolic, toxic and epileptic causes and always requires urgent comprehensive assessment.

clinicalComparison.title: Compare intact brainstem pathways with focal disruption
clinicalComparison.instruction: Link compact anatomy to the combination of cranial-nerve, long-tract, arousal and autonomic findings.

comparisons.label: Long-tract integrity

healthy.label: Continuous ascending and descending pathways
healthy.summary: Major motor and sensory tracts traverse the brainstem while maintaining organised transmission.
healthy.mechanism: Long fibres connect spinal, brainstem, thalamic and cortical levels.
healthy.observable: Motor and sensory function is consistent with intact tract conduction.

pathology.label: Focal long-tract interruption
pathology.summary: A compact lesion can affect descending motor or ascending sensory fibres together with nearby cranial-nerve systems.
pathology.mechanism: Dense tract packing allows a small lesion to disrupt multiple neighbouring pathways.
pathology.observable: Crossed or combined cranial-nerve and contralateral long-tract signs may appear.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: The combination of signs is usually more localising than any single symptom.
comparisons.assessment: Map side, modality and cranial-nerve involvement; abrupt onset or reduced consciousness requires urgent medical evaluation.
comparisons.caveat: Brainstem syndromes vary with lesion level, extent and vascular anatomy and are not reliably diagnosed from symptoms alone.

comparisons.label: Arousal systems

healthy.label: Sustained arousal regulation
healthy.summary: Brainstem arousal systems support wakefulness and modulate cortical state through widespread projections.
healthy.mechanism: Reticular and neuromodulatory systems interact with thalamic, hypothalamic and cortical targets.
healthy.observable: Wakefulness is maintained appropriately for sleep-wake state and context.

pathology.label: Arousal-system disruption
pathology.summary: Bilateral or strategically placed dysfunction can impair alertness and consciousness.
pathology.mechanism: Damage to ascending arousal pathways reduces effective activation of distributed forebrain systems.
pathology.observable: Somnolence, reduced alertness or more severe impairment of consciousness may occur.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: Altered consciousness is a medical sign with a broad differential; localisation is only one part of the assessment.
comparisons.assessment: Prioritise acute medical assessment, neurological examination and physiological causes before neuropsychological interpretation.
comparisons.caveat: Sedation, metabolic disturbance, seizure, sleep loss and diffuse brain dysfunction can also alter arousal.

assessmentLab.title: Assessment-linked brainstem reasoning
assessmentLab.instruction: Choose the most informative first assessment domain, then compare findings that would strengthen or weaken the localisation hypothesis.

cases.label: Long-tract pattern
cases.prompt: A patient develops new unilateral weakness with altered sensation and brisk reflexes after an acute neurological event. Which domain should be prioritised first?
cases.rationale: A long-tract hypothesis is tested most directly by the pattern of weakness, tone, reflexes, sensory change and side-to-side relationships before higher-order cognitive testing.
observe: sensory level or crossed sensory findings
supports: convergent cranial nerve or long-tract signs
challenges: inconsistent effort-dependent findings
a pattern better explained by peripheral nerve, neuromuscular or musculoskeletal pathology
absence of neurological signs despite a stable severe complaint
cases.nextStep: Escalate urgently for acute or progressive focal neurological signs; neuropsychological testing is secondary to medical localisation and stabilisation.
cases.caveat: Long-tract signs localise a system, not necessarily a single lesion. Brain, brainstem, spinal cord and mixed pathologies can produce overlapping patterns.

cases.label: Arousal / reticular pattern
cases.prompt: A patient is unusually difficult to rouse and shows fluctuating attention. What should come before formal cognitive testing?
cases.rationale: Reduced or fluctuating arousal can invalidate downstream cognitive testing and may signal an acute medical or neurological problem.
taskTypes: brief attention probes only when sufficiently alert
supports: temporal association with acute illness or medication change
challenges: stable alertness with selectively impaired cognition
a longstanding developmental attentional profile without altered consciousness
cases.nextStep: Treat altered consciousness as a medical assessment problem first; defer extensive neuropsychological testing until arousal is sufficiently stable.
cases.caveat: Arousal disturbance is highly non-specific and can arise from structural, metabolic, toxic, infectious, sleep-related and psychiatric causes.

integratedCaseLab.title: Integrated brainstem cases
integratedCaseLab.instruction: Work through localisation and assessment sequentially, then integrate supporting and conflicting evidence before committing to a formulation.

cases.label: Pontine crossed signs
cases.vignette: A patient develops sudden diplopia, ipsilateral facial weakness and contralateral limb weakness.
clues: cranial-nerve and long-tract signs occur together
limb weakness is contralateral to the facial findings
cases.hypothesisRationale: The combination of ipsilateral cranial-nerve findings with contralateral long-tract weakness is a classic crossed brainstem pattern and is more coherent with a pontine localisation than with an isolated peripheral lesion.
cases.assessmentRationale: Acute focal neurological signs require immediate medical localisation and stabilisation. Formal neuropsychological testing is secondary until the neurological state is characterised.
supports: reproducible gaze or facial motor abnormality
upper-motor-neuron limb pattern on the opposite side
challenges: facial weakness without any long-tract or ocular signs
peripheral nerve distribution better explains all findings
symptoms fluctuate without objective neurological signs
cases.synthesis: The crossed pattern raises a high-priority pontine hypothesis because neighbouring cranial-nerve nuclei/fascicles and descending long tracts can be affected together. The pattern should guide urgent neurological examination and imaging rather than stand alone as a diagnosis.
cases.nextStep: Escalate for acute neurological assessment and imaging; defer extensive cognitive testing until medically stable.
cases.caveat: Brainstem localisation is pattern-based and probabilistic. Exact vascular territory and structure require examination and imaging.

cases.label: Medullary swallowing pattern
cases.vignette: After an acute event, a patient has dysphagia, hoarse voice, gait unsteadiness and altered pain/temperature sensation affecting the face and opposite side of the body.
cases.hypothesisRationale: Dysphagia/hoarseness plus crossed pain-temperature findings and ataxia form a coherent medullary brainstem syndrome rather than an isolated cortical or peripheral pattern.
cases.targetAssessment: Swallow safety and focused neurological examination
assessmentOptions: Swallow safety and focused neurological examination
cases.assessmentRationale: Airway and swallowing risk take priority, followed by cranial-nerve, sensory, vestibular and cerebellar examination to establish the neurological pattern.
challenges: normal swallowing and cranial-nerve function
single peripheral sensory territory
isolated language or memory impairment
cases.synthesis: The convergent bulbar, sensory and cerebellar/vestibular signs support a medullary localisation. Clinical urgency is driven by swallowing and respiratory safety, not by neuropsychological profile.
cases.nextStep: Obtain urgent medical review, swallowing assessment and imaging as indicated.
cases.caveat: This teaching pattern is not a substitute for bedside localisation or acute stroke protocols.

brainstem-cerebellum.title: Brainstem & Cerebellum
brainstem-cerebellum.subtitle: Arousal, coordination and prediction
learningObjectives: Distinguish core brainstem roles in arousal, autonomic control, long tracts and cranial-nerve function.

sections.explainSimply: The brainstem keeps vital systems running and helps you stay awake. The cerebellum fine-tunes movement and helps the brain predict what happens next.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Brainstem nuclei regulate arousal, sleep, autonomic function and cranial nerves. Cerebellar circuits contribute to timing, error correction, learning and aspects of cognition and affect.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Ascending neuromodulatory systems influence global cortical state. Cerebello-thalamo-cortical loops support predictive modelling beyond motor control, including language, executive and affective regulation.
sections.thinkOfItLike: The brainstem is the power-and-alertness system; the cerebellum is a precision coach constantly comparing intended and actual performance.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Arousal and autonomic state can profoundly shape attention, emotion regulation and test performance.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Damage may cause altered consciousness, cranial nerve signs, ataxia, dysmetria or cognitive-affective changes.
sections.clinicalPearl: Before interpreting cognition, ask whether the person’s arousal and physiological state permit cognition to work normally.
sections.practicalExample: A person with acute diplopia, dysarthria and gait ataxia should not be conceptualised initially as having anxiety-related dizziness. The combination raises concern for posterior-circulation or brainstem–cerebellar pathology and requires urgent medical assessment.
sections.limitationsCautions: Cerebellar contributions to cognition and affect are real but should not be used to infer a specific cerebellar lesion from nonspecific executive or emotional symptoms. Acute cranial-nerve, consciousness or severe coordination changes require medical evaluation.

quizBank.question: Which structure is especially important for error correction and timing?
quizBank.explanation: The cerebellum compares predicted and actual outcomes to refine timing, coordination and learning.

reviewPrompts.answer: Brainstem nuclei regulate arousal, sleep, autonomic function and cranial nerves. Cerebellar circuits contribute to timing, error correction, learning and aspects of cognition and affect.

cell.title: The Cell
cell.subtitle: The smallest living unit
learningObjectives: Name the core cellular structures shared by neurons and glia.
Explain why ATP, protein synthesis and membrane integrity are prerequisites for neural signalling.
Relate cellular metabolic failure to changes in cognition and behaviour.

sections.explainSimply: Your brain is made of tiny living units called cells. Each cell is like a miniature workplace with a boundary, energy supply and instructions.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Neural tissue is cellular. Neurons and glia share core organelles, but specialise for signalling, support, defence and myelination.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The plasma membrane establishes electrochemical separation. The nucleus regulates gene expression; mitochondria generate ATP; ribosomes and endoplasmic reticulum synthesise proteins required for receptors, channels and structural maintenance.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A self-contained clinic: walls control entry, the records room stores instructions, and the generator powers every service.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Cellular energy failure, membrane instability and impaired protein handling can alter cognition, mood and behaviour before gross structural changes are visible.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Hypoxia, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation and toxic exposure can disrupt cellular metabolism and communication.
sections.clinicalPearl: Psychological function depends on biological systems that are active, adaptive and metabolically expensive.
sections.practicalExample: During hypoxia, reduced oxidative phosphorylation lowers ATP availability. Ion pumps then struggle to maintain gradients, so neural signalling can fail before there is a visible structural lesion.
sections.limitationsCautions: Cell biology explains mechanisms, not a person’s psychological presentation by itself. Clinical interpretation still requires timing, systemic physiology, examination and functional context.

quizBank.question: Which structure primarily controls what enters and leaves a cell?
quizBank.explanation: The plasma membrane selectively regulates movement between the cell and its environment.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Explain the cell in clinically useful terms.
reviewPrompts.answer: Neural tissue is cellular. Neurons and glia share core organelles, but specialise for signalling, support, defence and myelination.

cerebellum-atlas.title: Cerebellum Atlas
cerebellum-atlas.subtitle: Map lobules, peduncles, deep nuclei and cerebellar loops
cerebellum-atlas.altText: Interactive chalkboard-style anatomical atlas of Cerebellum with labelled regions and pathway relationships.
learningObjectives: Identify the cerebellar hemispheres, vermis, lobes, peduncles and deep nuclei.
Trace major input and output routes through cerebellar peduncles.
Explain motor and cognitive-affective consequences of cerebellar disruption.

sections.explainSimply: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement, timing and prediction. It also contributes to language, attention and emotional regulation through loops with the cortex.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Cerebellar function is best understood as error-based calibration across motor and cognitive systems, not merely balance and coordination.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Cerebellar cortex receives mossy- and climbing-fibre input, transforms signals through granule and Purkinje-cell circuitry, and modulates output through deep nuclei. Cerebello-thalamo-cortical loops support timing, prediction, adaptation and optimisation across motor and nonmotor domains.
sections.thinkOfItLike: It is the brain’s quality-control studio: it compares the intended performance with the actual performance and adjusts the next attempt.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Cerebellar lesions may produce cognitive-affective changes, slowed processing, dysprosody or executive inefficiency in addition to ataxia.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Assuming a normal strength examination excludes meaningful cerebellar dysfunction misses timing, coordination and cognitive-affective effects.
sections.clinicalPearl: The cerebellum does not initiate most behaviour; it calibrates the precision, timing and adaptability of behaviour.
sections.practicalExample: A posterior cerebellar lesion may leave basic strength intact yet produce dysmetria, slowed set-shifting and flattened affect.
sections.limitationsCautions: Cerebellar cognitive-affective findings are variable and should be corroborated with neurological signs, imaging and functional change.

cerebral-lobes-atlas.title: Cerebral Lobes Atlas
cerebral-lobes-atlas.subtitle: Compare frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital and insular territories
cerebral-lobes-atlas.altText: Interactive chalkboard-style anatomical atlas of Cerebral Lobes with labelled regions and pathway relationships.
learningObjectives: Identify the five major cerebral lobes in lateral and medial views.
Compare characteristic functions without reducing cognition to one lobe.
Relate cortical territories to blood supply and common lesion presentations.

sections.explainSimply: The cerebral cortex is divided into broad lobes that specialise in different kinds of information while continuously working together.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Lobe labels are useful orientation tools, but psychological functions arise from distributed networks that cross anatomical boundaries.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital and insular cortices contain multiple cytoarchitectonic and connectional territories. Clinical interpretation therefore depends on lesion location, laterality, white-matter disconnection and network compensation rather than lobe name alone.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of the lobes as districts in one city: each has characteristic services, but roads, utilities and people constantly cross district borders.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Lobe-level orientation helps psychologists connect behavioural change with plausible neural systems while avoiding crude localisation claims.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Treating one lobe as the sole home of a complex function can produce inaccurate formulation and overconfident lesion inference.
sections.clinicalPearl: Use lobes to orient; use networks, tracts and task demands to explain.
sections.practicalExample: A left posterior temporal lesion may disrupt language comprehension, but the person’s functional profile also depends on auditory processing, semantic networks and interhemispheric support.
sections.limitationsCautions: Individual variation is substantial. A lobe map cannot diagnose impairment or predict outcome without examination, imaging and functional assessment.

anatomy.outputs: Motor, striatal, thalamic, limbic and association-cortex outputs
anatomy.connections: Thalamic, limbic, sensory-association and contralateral cortical input; projects via Motor, striatal, thalamic, limbic and association-cortex outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Disinhibition, apathy, dysexecutive syndromes, motor deficits
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess frontal lobe in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Parietal lobe
anatomy.function: Multisensory integration, body representation, spatial attention and skilled action
anatomy.inputs: Somatosensory, visual, auditory and thalamic input
anatomy.outputs: Premotor, frontal, temporal and subcortical outputs
anatomy.connections: Somatosensory, visual, auditory and thalamic input; projects via Premotor, frontal, temporal and subcortical outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Neglect, apraxia, dyscalculia, somatosensory integration deficits
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess parietal lobe in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Temporal lobe
anatomy.function: Auditory analysis, semantic memory, object recognition and episodic-memory interfaces
anatomy.inputs: Auditory, visual, limbic and association-cortex input
anatomy.outputs: Frontal, parietal, limbic and subcortical outputs
anatomy.connections: Auditory, visual, limbic and association-cortex input; projects via Frontal, parietal, limbic and subcortical outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Aphasia, memory impairment, agnosia, altered emotion processing
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess temporal lobe in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Occipital lobe
anatomy.function: Early and intermediate visual analysis
anatomy.inputs: Thalamic visual input through the lateral geniculate nucleus
anatomy.connections: Thalamic visual input through the lateral geniculate nucleus; projects via Dorsal and ventral visual-stream outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Visual field loss, cortical blindness, visual perceptual deficits
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess occipital lobe in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.function: Interoception, salience, taste and integration of bodily state with emotion
anatomy.inputs: Visceral, somatosensory, limbic and thalamic input
anatomy.outputs: Cingulate, frontal, temporal, autonomic and subcortical outputs
anatomy.connections: Visceral, somatosensory, limbic and thalamic input; projects via Cingulate, frontal, temporal, autonomic and subcortical outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Altered interoception, taste disturbance, salience dysregulation
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess insula in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

cerebral-vasculature-atlas.title: Cerebral Vasculature Atlas
cerebral-vasculature-atlas.subtitle: Trace arterial territories, venous drainage, perforators and watershed zones
cerebral-vasculature-atlas.altText: Inferior and lateral brain views showing the Circle of Willis, anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries, perforators, watershed zones and venous drainage.
learningObjectives: Trace the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar circulations through the Circle of Willis.
Map ACA, MCA and PCA territories to characteristic neurobehavioural syndromes.
Recognise perforator, watershed and venous patterns that do not follow simple cortical territories.

sections.explainSimply: The brain receives blood through two paired arterial systems that join at its base and branch across the surface and deep structures.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Vascular territory often predicts the pattern and timing of cognitive, language, emotional and behavioural change, but collateral flow and individual anatomy create variability.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Anterior circulation derives primarily from internal carotid arteries; posterior circulation from vertebral arteries joining the basilar artery. The Circle of Willis permits collateral redistribution. Cortical branches, deep perforators and border zones produce distinct lesion patterns.
sections.thinkOfItLike: It is a city water network: major mains, ring connections, neighbourhood branches and tiny deep supply pipes each fail in different ways.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Sudden focal cognitive or behavioural change is a neurological emergency. Aphasia, neglect, amnesia or disinhibition may be the presenting sign of stroke.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Assuming stroke always presents with obvious weakness may miss posterior, right-hemisphere or strategically located infarcts.
sections.clinicalPearl: Territory maps are probabilistic: variant anatomy and collateral circulation can substantially alter the clinical picture.
sections.practicalExample: A dominant-hemisphere superior-division MCA infarct may produce nonfluent aphasia with relatively preserved comprehension.
sections.limitationsCautions: This atlas cannot determine an individual vascular lesion; acute symptoms require emergency stroke assessment and imaging.

anatomy.label: Circle of Willis
anatomy.function: Provides an arterial collateral ring at the brain base
anatomy.connections: Anterior and posterior communicating arteries
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Anatomical completeness varies; collateral competence cannot be assumed.

anatomy.label: Anterior cerebral artery
anatomy.function: Supplies medial frontal and parietal cortex
anatomy.connections: Corpus callosum and medial motor regions
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Medial frontal injury may look psychiatric or motivational.

anatomy.label: Middle cerebral artery
anatomy.function: Supplies much of lateral cerebral cortex and deep lenticulostriate territories
anatomy.outputs: Superior, inferior and deep perforating divisions
anatomy.connections: Language, attention, motor and sensory networks
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: MCA syndromes vary markedly by hemisphere and division.

anatomy.label: Posterior cerebral artery
anatomy.function: Supplies occipital, inferomedial temporal and thalamic regions
anatomy.inputs: Basilar apex or fetal-origin internal carotid
anatomy.connections: Visual cortex, hippocampal and thalamic systems
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Visual field loss, alexia, memory disturbance
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Posterior lesions can produce profound cognitive symptoms with little motor weakness.

anatomy.label: Watershed zones
anatomy.function: Border regions vulnerable to systemic hypoperfusion
anatomy.inputs: Distal ACA, MCA and PCA branches
anatomy.connections: High-order association cortex
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Proximal limb weakness or higher cognitive deficits may follow hypotension.

anatomy.label: Deep perforators
anatomy.function: Supply internal capsule, basal ganglia, thalamus and brainstem
anatomy.inputs: MCA, ACA, PCA and basilar branches
anatomy.connections: Compact motor, sensory and arousal pathways
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Lacunar infarcts and strategic thalamic syndromes
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Small lesions can cause dense deficits because deep pathways are tightly packed.

chemistry.title: Brain Chemistry
chemistry.subtitle: Messages across microscopic gaps
learningObjectives: Describe synthesis, vesicular release, receptor binding and signal termination in chemical neurotransmission.
Explain why transmitter effects depend on receptor subtype, circuit and timing.
Reject the simplistic “single chemical imbalance” model of psychiatric symptoms.

sections.explainSimply: Neurons often pass messages by releasing chemicals into a tiny gap. The next cell reads the chemical with matching receptors.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Neurotransmission depends on synthesis, vesicular release, receptor binding and signal termination through reuptake, diffusion or enzymatic breakdown.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Calcium influx at the presynaptic terminal triggers SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion. Postsynaptic effects vary by receptor subtype, intracellular signalling and the receiving cell’s current state.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A keycard system: the same messenger can open one door, lock another, or do nothing when the reader is absent.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: “Chemical imbalance” is an inadequate clinical model. Symptoms arise from dynamic circuits, learning, physiology and context—not a single low or high transmitter.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Receptor dysregulation, impaired clearance, medication interactions and substance use can alter signalling across multiple networks.
sections.clinicalPearl: A neurotransmitter has no fixed psychological meaning outside its receptor, circuit, timing and context.
sections.practicalExample: Serotonin can produce different effects in different circuits because receptor families couple to different intracellular pathways and are expressed on different cell types.
sections.limitationsCautions: Neurotransmitter measures at the group level do not diagnose an individual. Psychological symptoms emerge from interacting circuits, development, learning, physiology and context.

quizBank.question: What directly triggers vesicle release at the presynaptic terminal?
quizBank.explanation: Incoming action potentials open voltage-gated calcium channels, initiating vesicle fusion and transmitter release.

chronic-stress-trauma.title: Chronic Stress
chronic-stress-trauma.subtitle: When repeated demand reshapes regulation
chronic-stress-trauma.altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating chronic stress across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain chronic stress in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in chronic stress.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to chronic stress.

sections.explainSimply: Chronic stress keeps protective systems active too often or for too long.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Repeated activation can alter sleep, attention, emotion regulation, immune signalling and learning while increasing avoidance and exhaustion.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Allostatic load describes cumulative regulatory cost, but it is a population-level construct rather than a clinical diagnostic test.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of chronic stress as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need chronic stress to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not attribute every symptom to cortisol or “nervous-system dysregulation.”
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use chronic stress to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses chronic stress to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not attribute every symptom to cortisol or “nervous-system dysregulation.” Evidence classification: established concept; individual effects vary.

sections.explainSimply: The cingulate cortex curves around the corpus callosum and helps connect motivation, pain, attention, memory and emotion.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Different cingulate zones participate in salience, action selection, autonomic regulation, error monitoring and internally directed cognition.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Anterior and midcingulate sectors connect strongly with prefrontal, insular, limbic, motor and autonomic systems; posterior cingulate and retrosplenial regions are central nodes in memory and default-mode networks. Boundaries are functional gradients rather than rigid boxes.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A bridge running around the brain’s central highway, linking body state, motivation, action and memory.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Cingulate lesions may alter initiation, error monitoring, affect, pain experience, memory orientation or self-referential processing depending on location and connectivity.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Damage or dysregulation can disrupt salience network, default mode network, pain matrix; presentations depend on laterality, extent and connected networks.
sections.clinicalPearl: “Cingulate dysfunction” is too broad to be clinically useful—specify the subregion, network and task demand.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses the cingulate cortex atlas map to test whether a patient’s pattern is anatomically coherent while considering broader network and medical explanations.
sections.limitationsCautions: Atlas localisation supports hypothesis generation, not diagnosis. Individual anatomy, distributed processing, compensation and comorbidity limit one-to-one structure–symptom claims.

anatomy.position: Integrated within deep or medial cortical-brainstem relationships shown in the atlas.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the cingulate cortex atlas?
options: Different cingulate zones participate in salience, action selection, autonomic regulation, error monitoring and internally directed cognition.
It acts independently of the rest of the brain.
It has one fixed psychological function.
It can diagnose psychiatric disorders from anatomy alone.
quiz.rationale: The structure participates in distributed networks and should be interpreted in context.

quiz.question: What is the safest clinical inference from this atlas?
options: A lesion pattern can guide hypotheses but requires clinical and medical correlation.
One symptom proves one structure is damaged.
quiz.rationale: Neuroanatomy constrains hypotheses but does not replace assessment.

quiz.question: Why are connections important?
options: Symptoms can reflect disconnection and downstream network effects.
All pathways are identical across people.
quiz.rationale: Distributed cognitive systems depend on pathways linking regions.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the core clinical distinction?
reviewPrompts.answer: The strongest localisation comes from a coherent pattern across functions, time course and examination—not from one low test score.

High-value reasoning moves from syndrome to anatomical hypothesis, then tests vascular territory, tract, network and differential diagnosis. Double dissociations support functional architecture, but real patients show distributed and overlapping deficits. Cognitive findings must be interpreted alongside effort, fatigue, language, mood, pain, medications, premorbid ability and ecological validity.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What red flags or alternatives matter?
reviewPrompts.answer: Acute focal deficit, thunderclap headache, new seizure, rapidly progressive cognitive change or fluctuating consciousness requires urgent medical assessment. Do not overlocalise nonspecific symptoms.

sections.whenItGoesWrong: A sophisticated display cannot compensate for a contaminated signal.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using closed-loop systems predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: A sophisticated display cannot compensate for a contaminated signal. Evidence classification: established engineering principle.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the core clinical distinction?
reviewPrompts.answer: A child who cannot formulate language efficiently may look inattentive, oppositional or socially awkward when the primary bottleneck is communication.

Network development is shaped by genetic liability, auditory-linguistic exposure, motor planning and social interaction. There is no single “language centre” or diagnostic scan. Profiles are often uneven and overlap with ADHD, autism, dyslexia, hearing impairment and intellectual disability. Bilingualism does not cause language disorder; impairment should be evident across the child’s languages relative to exposure.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What red flags or alternatives matter?
reviewPrompts.answer: New aphasia, facial weakness, dysarthria or abrupt speech change requires urgent neurological assessment. Persistent communication difficulty should not be attributed to bilingualism without evidence across languages.

sections.explainSimply: Cranial Nerves is a set of connected structures that can be explored layer by layer to understand where it sits and what it does.

sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Recognising plausible neuroanatomical patterns supports better referral, formulation and interpretation of cognitive or behavioural change.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Over-localising a symptom to one structure, or treating an atlas view as diagnostic evidence, can produce false certainty.
sections.clinicalPearl: The only sensory system that reaches cortex without an obligatory thalamic relay.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician can select a structure in the Cranial Nerves Atlas and trace its inputs and outputs before comparing the predicted pattern with examination, imaging and functional assessment.
sections.limitationsCautions: This atlas supports learning and clinical reasoning; it does not replace neurological examination, imaging or specialist interpretation.

anatomy.label: CN I — Olfactory
anatomy.function: Smell
anatomy.connections: Olfactory epithelium; projects to Olfactory bulb and cortex.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: The only sensory system that reaches cortex without an obligatory thalamic relay.

anatomy.label: CN II — Optic
anatomy.function: Vision
anatomy.outputs: Chiasm, tract, LGN and visual cortex
anatomy.connections: Retinal ganglion cells; projects to Chiasm, tract, LGN and visual cortex.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Field defects localise lesions along the visual pathway.

anatomy.label: CN III, IV and VI
anatomy.function: Coordinate eye movements and pupil responses
anatomy.connections: Brainstem gaze systems; projects to Extraocular muscles and pupil.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Patterns of ophthalmoplegia help localise brainstem, cavernous sinus or orbital disease.

anatomy.label: CN V — Trigeminal
anatomy.function: Facial sensation and mastication
anatomy.outputs: Brainstem nuclei and muscles of mastication
anatomy.connections: Face, cornea, oral cavity; projects to Brainstem nuclei and muscles of mastication.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Corneal reflex testing samples both trigeminal and facial pathways.

anatomy.label: CN VII — Facial
anatomy.function: Facial expression, taste, lacrimation and salivation
anatomy.connections: Pons and taste receptors; projects to Facial muscles and glands.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Forehead sparing suggests a supranuclear lesion rather than peripheral facial palsy.

anatomy.label: CN VIII — Vestibulocochlear
anatomy.function: Hearing and balance
anatomy.connections: Cochlea and vestibular organs; projects to Pontomedullary nuclei.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Peripheral and central vestibular signs require different urgency and interpretation.

anatomy.label: CN IX and X
anatomy.function: Swallowing, voice and visceral regulation
anatomy.connections: Pharynx, larynx and viscera; projects to Nucleus ambiguus and autonomic nuclei.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: New bulbar symptoms can signal urgent brainstem or neuromuscular disease.

anatomy.label: CN XI and XII
anatomy.function: Head turning, shoulder elevation and tongue movement
anatomy.connections: Motor nuclei; projects to SCM, trapezius and tongue.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Tongue deviation and atrophy help distinguish lower from upper motor pathway lesions.

sections.explainSimply: EMDR is an evidence-based trauma-focused psychotherapy for PTSD and is recommended in major clinical guidance.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Comparative evidence does not show EMDR to be consistently superior to other bona fide psychological treatments for PTSD; treatment preference, fit, access and dropout still matter.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The evidence supports EMDR as a treatment approach for PTSD, not a uniquely proven neural mechanism. Mechanistic accounts—including working-memory taxation, orienting responses and memory updating—remain active areas of research.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of current evidence base as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need current evidence base to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Guideline support does not mean universal benefit or zero risk.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use current evidence base to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses current evidence base to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Guideline support establishes treatment legitimacy, not universal benefit, superiority over every alternative, or a uniquely established neural mechanism. Evidence classification: established PTSD treatment efficacy; mechanism uncertainty remains.
