learningObjectives: Identify the major components of deep nuclei.

sections.explainSimply: Deep Nuclei is a set of connected structures that can be explored layer by layer to understand where it sits and what it does.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: This atlas links the anatomy of deep nuclei to behaviour, cognition, neurological signs and clinically meaningful patterns without reducing complex functions to one structure.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The deep nuclei should be interpreted through spatial relationships, laterality, vascular supply, pathway continuity and distributed network effects. Focal damage can create both local signs and disconnection syndromes.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of it as a layered transit map: structures are stations, tracts are routes, and symptoms depend on which junctions or connections are interrupted.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Recognising plausible neuroanatomical patterns supports better referral, formulation and interpretation of cognitive or behavioural change.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Over-localising a symptom to one structure, or treating an atlas view as diagnostic evidence, can produce false certainty.
sections.clinicalPearl: Its head, body and tail curve with the lateral ventricle.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician can select a structure in the Deep Nuclei Atlas and trace its inputs and outputs before comparing the predicted pattern with examination, imaging and functional assessment.
sections.limitationsCautions: This atlas supports learning and clinical reasoning; it does not replace neurological examination, imaging or specialist interpretation.

anatomy.label: Caudate nucleus
anatomy.function: Action selection, learning and cognitive loops
anatomy.connections: Cortex and substantia nigra; projects to Globus pallidus and substantia nigra.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Its head, body and tail curve with the lateral ventricle.

anatomy.label: Putamen
anatomy.function: Motor and habit-related striatal processing
anatomy.connections: Motor and somatosensory cortex; projects to Globus pallidus and substantia nigra.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: The putamen is the lateral part of the dorsal striatum.

anatomy.label: Globus pallidus
anatomy.function: Major inhibitory output and relay of basal-ganglia loops
anatomy.connections: Striatum and subthalamic nucleus; projects to Thalamus and brainstem.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Internal and external segments have different roles in direct and indirect pathways.

anatomy.label: Subthalamic nucleus
anatomy.function: Excitatory control of pallidal output
anatomy.connections: Cortex and external pallidum; projects to Internal pallidum and substantia nigra.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: A small lesion can cause dramatic contralateral flinging movements.

anatomy.label: Substantia nigra
anatomy.function: Dopamine modulation and basal-ganglia output
anatomy.connections: Striatum and subthalamic nucleus; projects to Striatum, thalamus and brainstem.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Pars compacta and pars reticulata serve distinct modulatory and output functions.

anatomy.label: Thalamic nuclei
anatomy.function: Relay and regulate sensory, motor and associative information
anatomy.inputs: Cortex, basal ganglia, cerebellum and sensory pathways
anatomy.connections: Cortex, basal ganglia, cerebellum and sensory pathways; projects to Cerebral cortex.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: The thalamus is a family of nuclei, not a single relay station.

anatomy.label: Claustrum
anatomy.function: Widespread cortical integration; function remains uncertain
anatomy.connections: Broad cortical input; projects to Broad cortical output.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Its extensive connectivity is established, but strong claims about consciousness remain speculative.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the central mechanism in this concept?
reviewPrompts.answer: Findings implicate insular, striatal, frontoparietal and limbic circuitry, but there is no diagnostic neural signature. Restriction may become negatively reinforcing by reducing anxiety; repeated behaviours become habitual; prediction errors around food and body cues may be distorted. Energy deficiency changes dopamine, serotonin, endocrine function and network efficiency. Weight restoration can reverse some abnormalities, while trait vulnerabilities may remain.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the most important clinical caution?
reviewPrompts.answer: The starving brain cannot be interpreted as if it were metabolically neutral; state effects and trait vulnerability must be separated.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What alternative explanations or red flags must be considered?
reviewPrompts.answer: Bradycardia, syncope, electrolyte disturbance, dehydration, haematemesis, severe weakness, acute food refusal or escalating suicidality require urgent medical review. Refeeding syndrome is a medical emergency risk in severely malnourished patients.

electricity.title: Brain Electricity
electricity.subtitle: Voltage created by ions
learningObjectives: Explain membrane voltage in terms of ion gradients and conductance.
Distinguish postsynaptic potentials from action potentials and population-level EEG signals.
Relate excitation–inhibition balance to network stability without reducing it to a single transmitter.

sections.explainSimply: Brain electricity is not like a wire in a wall. It comes from charged particles moving through tiny gates in cell membranes.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Membrane voltage reflects unequal ion distribution. Excitatory and inhibitory inputs shift the probability that a neuron will generate an action potential.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Resting potential is dominated by potassium leak conductance and maintained gradients. Depolarisation toward threshold recruits voltage-gated sodium channels; repolarisation follows sodium inactivation and potassium efflux.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A stadium wave: each person moves locally, but the organised pattern travels across the crowd.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: EEG reflects summed postsynaptic activity from synchronised cortical populations, not single-neuron action potentials.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Excess excitation, reduced inhibition or disturbed ion balance can destabilise networks and increase seizure risk.
sections.clinicalPearl: Electrical activity is the medium; information is carried by timing, pattern, location and network context.
sections.practicalExample: A scalp EEG rhythm reflects synchronised postsynaptic currents across aligned cortical populations. It does not represent individual neurons firing like wires beneath each electrode.
sections.limitationsCautions: Electrical recordings are shaped by source geometry, synchrony, volume conduction, reference choice and state. A waveform alone does not specify a psychological process or diagnosis.

quizBank.explanation: Scalp EEG mainly captures synchronised postsynaptic currents generated by large cortical populations.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the central mechanism in this concept?
reviewPrompts.answer: Epileptogenesis reflects altered excitation–inhibition balance, ion-channel function, synaptic organisation, gliosis and network connectivity. Seizure initiation and spread depend on local circuitry and large-scale propagation pathways. Interictal discharges can disrupt processing transiently. EEG supports classification but a normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy, and incidental abnormalities do not establish diagnosis without clinical correlation.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the most important clinical caution?
reviewPrompts.answer: Epilepsy is a network disorder, not simply “too much electricity.” Do not diagnose seizure type from appearance alone, and do not equate functional seizures with faking.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What alternative explanations or red flags must be considered?
reviewPrompts.answer: Prolonged seizures, repeated seizures without recovery, injury, pregnancy or first seizure require urgent medical evaluation. Sudden unexplained death in epilepsy is uncommon but clinically important; adherence, nocturnal supervision discussions and seizure control matter.

mechanismMap.label: Core function
mechanismMap.detail: Episodic memory helps you remember events and information from a particular time and place. Learning, storing and retrieving are separate steps.

mechanismMap.label: Neural systems
mechanismMap.detail: The medial temporal system supports relational binding and consolidation, while prefrontal systems organise encoding and strategic retrieval. A rapid-forgetting pattern despite adequate learning may suggest storage dysfunction; improvement with cues may indicate retrieval inefficiency. These patterns are probabilistic and must be interpreted with base rates, effort and context.

mechanismMap.label: Assessment pattern
mechanismMap.detail: Neuropsychological interpretation distinguishes encoding, consolidation, storage and retrieval. Learning slope, delayed retention, recognition, intrusion errors and cueing effects help identify where the process breaks down. Attention and executive organisation strongly affect initial learning.

mechanismMap.label: Clinical translation
mechanismMap.detail: Different memory profiles imply different supports. Encoding problems benefit from simplification and repetition; retrieval problems benefit from cueing and structure; storage problems require stronger external compensation and medical investigation.

sections.explainSimply: Ethical practice explains what is known, uncertain, burdensome and alternative.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Clinicians should work within competence, protect EEG privacy, disclose costs and conflicts, use validated outcomes and avoid diagnostic or curative claims unsupported by evidence.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: CRED-nf standards support transparent experimental reporting. Clinical services should similarly document protocol, adverse events, concurrent care and meaningful outcomes.

sections.whenItGoesWrong: Precision in uncertainty is a clinical skill, not a marketing weakness.
sections.clinicalPearl: Measure benefit and harm with the same seriousness.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using ethics, evidence and clinical limits predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Precision in uncertainty is a clinical skill, not a marketing weakness. Evidence classification: established ethical standards; evidence varies by indication.

sections.explainSimply: Overlay default-mode, salience, executive, dorsal-attention and sensorimotor systems.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Network models fit transdiagnostic formulation better than single-region explanations, but resting-state correlations are not direct measures of thoughts or diagnoses.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Location: Large-scale networks span noncontiguous cortical and subcortical nodes, often overlapping within hub regions. Major subdivisions include default mode network, salience network, frontoparietal control network, dorsal attention network, ventral attention network, sensorimotor network, visual network, limbic network. Inputs include sensory systems, interoceptive signals, memory systems, task goals, reward and threat signals; outputs include motor systems, autonomic systems, memory updating, attention allocation, goal-directed behaviour.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A dynamic transport and control map: the meaning of any node depends on the routes entering, leaving and bypassing it.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Network models fit transdiagnostic formulation better than single-region explanations, but resting-state correlations are not direct measures of thoughts or diagnoses.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Damage or dysconnectivity may disturb attention, self-related thought, executive control, awareness or behaviour. Similar symptoms can arise from different nodes, and one lesion can affect several networks.
sections.clinicalPearl: Ask which network should dominate for the task, which network should disengage, and whether switching between them is efficient.
sections.practicalExample: Select a region, trace its incoming and outgoing pathways, then compare healthy and lesion overlays before forming a clinical hypothesis.
sections.limitationsCautions: Network boundaries depend on analytic method, task, arousal and individual variability. Functional connectivity is statistical dependence, not proof of direct anatomical connection or causal influence.

anatomy.label: Nodes
anatomy.short: Regions or parcels represented in a network
anatomy.detail: Nodes may be anatomical regions, functionally defined parcels or recording sites. Their meaning depends on how the network was constructed.
anatomy.clinical: Changing the parcellation can change apparent network organisation.

anatomy.label: Edges
anatomy.detail: Edges represent relationships such as correlation, coherence or tract connectivity.
anatomy.clinical: A functional edge does not establish direct communication or causal direction.

anatomy.label: Hubs
anatomy.detail: Some regions connect many systems and may support integration across specialised processes.
anatomy.clinical: Hub vulnerability can have widespread effects despite a small focal lesion.

anatomy.label: Segregation
anatomy.detail: Networks balance within-system cohesion with separation from other systems.
anatomy.clinical: Too little or too much segregation can reduce adaptive flexibility.

anatomy.label: Integration
anatomy.detail: Integration allows information to move between specialised networks as goals change.
anatomy.clinical: Complex tasks often require transient increases in cross-network coordination.

anatomy.label: Dynamic states
anatomy.short: Connectivity changes over seconds to longer periods
anatomy.detail: Networks reconfigure with task, arousal, learning and internal state.
anatomy.clinical: A static average may conceal clinically meaningful fluctuations.

healthy-versus-pathology-comparison.title: Healthy Versus Pathology Comparison
healthy-versus-pathology-comparison.subtitle: Compare variation, dysfunction, injury and disorder without treating a scan as a diagnosis
healthy-versus-pathology-comparison.altText: Accessible chalkboard-style comparison of two overlapping brain network maps: one shows variable healthy organisation and the other shows structural, functional, developmental, vascular and degenerative patterns, joined by a clinical-context bridge.
learningObjectives: Distinguish healthy variation, dysfunction, injury and disorder using clinical context rather than a binary normal-abnormal label.
Compare structural, functional, developmental, vascular and degenerative patterns without assuming that imaging establishes diagnosis.
Interpret symptoms through distributed networks, pathways, time course and reserve.
Identify limitations and uncertainty when relating a biological finding to a person's presentation.

sections.explainSimply: Healthy brains vary. A difference on a scan may be harmless, while important dysfunction may occur without a visible structural lesion. Pathology becomes clinically meaningful through pattern, time course, symptoms and context.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Variation describes differences within expected diversity; dysfunction is impaired operation; injury is damage caused by an event; disorder is a clinically defined syndrome involving distress, impairment or risk. These categories overlap but are not interchangeable, and none can be inferred from imaging alone.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Comparison requires converging evidence from history, examination, cognitive or psychological assessment, laboratory data, structural and functional imaging, longitudinal change and differential diagnosis. Structural abnormalities may be incidental; functional changes may be state-dependent or nonspecific; developmental organisation may differ without representing acquired damage; vascular lesions follow time and territory; degenerative disease is supported by progressive clinical and biomarker patterns. Network disconnection, diaschisis, compensation, reserve and comorbidity shape phenotype.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A city map and a traffic report: street layout, current flow, construction damage and long-term decline describe different things, and none alone tells you how one resident is functioning.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Careful framing prevents biological essentialism, false reassurance from an unremarkable scan, and overdiagnosis from incidental findings. It supports formulation that integrates cognition, emotion, behaviour, daily function, development and medical context.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Acute infarction can disrupt a vascularly organised network; traumatic axonal injury can disconnect systems beyond a focal lesion; epilepsy, migraine or metabolic disturbance can alter function transiently; developmental differences shape network organisation; degeneration evolves across connected systems. Similar symptoms can arise through different mechanisms, and similar findings can have different consequences.
sections.clinicalPearl: Treat imaging as one source of evidence: ask whether the finding, time course, network and examination converge before attributing a symptom or diagnosis.
sections.practicalExample: Compare an incidental small arachnoid cyst in a well person, transient network dysfunction during migraine aura, focal tissue injury after an MCA infarct, a developmental language disorder and progressive medial temporal-network degeneration. The clinically useful distinction comes from convergence, not appearance alone.
sections.limitationsCautions: Normal ranges depend on age, development, acquisition method and reference population. Group-level biomarkers often overlap across individuals and diagnoses. Absence of a visible lesion does not exclude dysfunction, while an abnormal-looking finding may be incidental. Avoid value-laden language and deterministic normal-versus-abnormal conclusions.

anatomy.position: Whole-brain comparison across cortex, subcortex, white matter, vascular territories and large-scale functional networks.
anatomy.spatialRelationships: Local tissue findings sit within connected systems; remote effects may occur through white-matter disconnection, diaschisis, altered excitation-inhibition balance and compensatory recruitment.
outputs: need for monitoring or urgent action
anatomy.bloodSupply: Vascular change is interpreted by onset, arterial territory, collateral supply and tissue evolution. Chronic small-vessel disease and incidental vascular variants require clinical correlation.
anatomy.lesionEffects: Effects depend on lesion mechanism, location, volume, laterality, white-matter involvement, distributed network disruption, premorbid reserve and recovery; a lesion does not map one-to-one onto a symptom.
psychologicalPresentations: distress shaped by interpretation and context
no impairment despite an incidental finding
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: A healthy-pathology comparison can organise hypotheses and urgency, but diagnosis requires concordance among clinical phenotype, course, examination and appropriately interpreted tests.

explorerParts.label: Healthy variation & reserve
explorerParts.detail: Brain morphology, lateralisation, connectivity and performance vary with age, development, experience and measurement conditions.
explorerParts.clinical: Use appropriate norms and functional evidence before labelling a variant pathological.

explorerParts.label: Structural change
explorerParts.detail: Atrophy, mass effect, altered signal, malformation or white-matter change describes structure, not by itself cause, severity or diagnosis.
explorerParts.clinical: Correlate location and chronicity with symptoms; consider incidental findings, artefact and alternative causes.

explorerParts.label: Functional dysfunction
explorerParts.short: Operation can change without a fixed lesion
explorerParts.detail: Network physiology can vary with seizure activity, migraine, medication, sleep, pain, metabolic state and psychiatric state.
explorerParts.clinical: Functional measures are often state-dependent and group-derived; they should support rather than replace clinical assessment.

explorerParts.label: Developmental difference
explorerParts.detail: Developmental timing, plasticity and experience shape network organisation and skill acquisition across childhood and adulthood.
explorerParts.clinical: Establish developmental history and adaptive impact; avoid describing all atypical organisation as damage.

explorerParts.label: Vascular injury
explorerParts.detail: Ischaemia and haemorrhage disrupt tissue according to vessel anatomy, collateral flow, lesion evolution and connected pathways.
explorerParts.clinical: Sudden focal deficits require urgent stroke assessment; imaging pattern assists but does not replace bedside evaluation.

explorerParts.label: Degenerative network change
explorerParts.detail: Neurodegenerative processes often spread through vulnerable cell populations and connected networks rather than respecting one isolated region.
explorerParts.clinical: Diagnosis depends on progressive phenotype, exclusion of mimics and, when appropriate, validated biomarkers.

quiz.question: Which description of dysfunction is most accurate?
options: Impaired operation may occur with or without a visible structural lesion
It always means irreversible tissue destruction
It is identical to a disorder
It can be inferred from one group-average biomarker
quiz.rationale: Physiological dysfunction may be transient, state-dependent or structurally occult and is not synonymous with injury or disorder.

Every symptom belongs to one brain region
quiz.rationale: Clinical effects emerge from distributed systems and individual context, not lesion location alone.

quiz.rationale: Degenerative diagnosis rests on progression and converging clinical evidence, sometimes supported by validated biomarkers.

cases.label: Incidental
cases.prompt: Imaging shows a stable anatomical variant, but the person has no concordant neurological signs, cognitive decline or functional change.
cases.rationale: A structural difference without a concordant clinical phenotype may represent healthy variation or an incidental finding rather than disease.
cases.caveat: Clinical significance depends on the specific finding, history and appropriate medical interpretation.

cases.label: Acute focal
cases.prompt: A previously well person develops sudden unilateral weakness and language difficulty over minutes.
cases.rationale: A sudden focal neurological syndrome is a vascular emergency pattern until proven otherwise, and time course is as important as location.
cases.caveat: Stroke mimics exist, but emergency assessment should not be delayed while attempting to resolve the differential.

cases.label: Progressive
cases.prompt: Cognitive and behavioural abilities decline progressively over years with increasing functional dependence and a coherent network-level pattern.
cases.rationale: A progressive, patterned decline raises a neurodegenerative hypothesis, which is evaluated longitudinally alongside reversible causes and, when indicated, biomarkers.
cases.caveat: Progressive symptoms do not identify a specific disease by themselves; psychiatric, medical, medication and sleep-related contributors require assessment.

clinicalComparison.title: Compare normal variation with disrupted systems
clinicalComparison.instruction: Switch between qualified examples. Keep normal variation, compensation and context separate from pathology.

comparisons.label: Functional network change

healthy.label: Flexible network recruitment
healthy.summary: Distributed systems change their coupling with task demands and state.
healthy.mechanism: Dynamic recruitment and inhibition support efficient switching between networks.
healthy.observable: Performance varies with task load while core function remains broadly adaptive.

pathology.label: Inefficient or disrupted recruitment
pathology.summary: A network may become less efficient, less selective or poorly coordinated with other systems.
pathology.mechanism: Altered connectivity, node dysfunction or state effects can disturb coordinated processing.
pathology.observable: Slowed, inconsistent or context-sensitive cognitive performance may emerge.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: The clinically useful question is not whether a network looks different, but whether the difference converges with history, examination and functional impairment.
comparisons.assessment: Compare performance across tasks and contexts, look for converging cognitive patterns, and consider fatigue, mood, medication and validity.
comparisons.caveat: Functional differences are not diagnostic biomarkers on their own and may reflect state, development, compensation or measurement noise.

comparisons.label: Vascular disruption

healthy.label: Intact perfusion
healthy.summary: Neural tissue receives sufficient blood flow to support local computation and connected network function.
healthy.mechanism: Arterial supply and autoregulation maintain oxygen and substrate delivery.
healthy.observable: No focal deficit attributable to acute regional hypoperfusion.

pathology.label: Focal vascular injury
pathology.summary: Ischaemia or haemorrhage can damage local tissue and interrupt fibres passing through the region.
pathology.mechanism: Tissue injury plus oedema, disconnection and remote network effects shape the phenotype.
pathology.observable: Abrupt focal neurological and cognitive changes may occur, depending on territory and extent.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: Time course and neurological pattern are central to vascular reasoning; the same cognitive symptom can arise from different territories or mechanisms.
comparisons.assessment: Pair neuropsychological findings with onset, neurological signs, imaging and vascular history rather than reverse-inferring a lesion from a test score.
comparisons.caveat: Vascular territories overlap and symptoms evolve with reperfusion, oedema, diaschisis and recovery.

comparisons.label: Degenerative change

healthy.label: Age-related change
healthy.summary: Some slowing and variability can occur with ageing without constituting neurodegenerative disease.
healthy.mechanism: Normal ageing involves heterogeneous biological and cognitive changes with substantial individual variation.
healthy.observable: Mild slowing may coexist with preserved everyday independence and stable learned knowledge.

pathology.label: Progressive neurodegenerative pattern
pathology.summary: Disease processes progressively compromise vulnerable neural systems and connected functions.
pathology.mechanism: Pathology accumulates over time and affects networks according to disease-specific and individual factors.
pathology.observable: Progressive decline, loss of previously established abilities and increasing functional impact may appear.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: Trajectory and loss of function matter more than a single low score when distinguishing normal variation from progressive disease.
comparisons.assessment: Use collateral history, serial change, functional status, medical work-up and domain pattern alongside normative interpretation.
comparisons.caveat: Age, education, sensory factors, mood, sleep, medication and premorbid ability can mimic or magnify apparent decline.

assessmentLab.title: Assessment-linked healthy/pathology reasoning
assessmentLab.instruction: Use trajectory, functional impact and converging evidence to distinguish variation from clinically significant change.

cases.label: Functional change
cases.prompt: A person reports cognitive difficulty but structural imaging is unremarkable. What assessment domain best determines whether there is meaningful dysfunction?
cases.rationale: Normal structural imaging does not exclude dysfunction; significance comes from reproducible cognitive/behavioural change, time course and real-world impact.
supports: objective change converging with functional decline
time course compatible with the hypothesised mechanism
challenges: stable lifelong profile
symptoms tracking primarily with sleep, stress or medication state
lack of functional impact despite subjective concern
cases.nextStep: Use longitudinal and multimethod evidence; investigate reversible contributors and do not treat a normal scan as proof of normal function.
cases.caveat: Objective tests can also be normal despite genuine intermittent or context-dependent impairment; absence of a test abnormality is not proof that symptoms are unreal.

cases.label: Vascular change
cases.prompt: A patient develops abrupt focal cognitive and neurological change. What should anchor the assessment?
cases.targetDomain: Time-locked focal neurological and cognitive profile
options: Time-locked focal neurological and cognitive profile
cases.rationale: Abrupt onset and focal signs make vascular localisation and urgent medical assessment higher priority than broad trait-level psychological interpretation.
observe: focal weakness, sensory or visual signs
vascular risk and acute medical context
taskTypes: brief focal cognitive screening when medically appropriate
later targeted neuropsychological assessment for recovery planning
challenges: gradual longstanding course
non-focal fluctuating symptoms better explained by systemic state
discordant anatomy and symptom timing
cases.nextStep: Acute stroke-like presentations require emergency medical pathways; detailed neuropsychological assessment follows stabilisation.
cases.caveat: Small, strategic or posterior-circulation events can be clinically significant despite subtle early findings.

cases.label: Degenerative change
cases.prompt: A family reports gradual progressive decline over several years. Which assessment feature is most informative for distinguishing disease-related change from stable individual variation?
options: A single low score in isolation
cases.rationale: Neurodegenerative hypotheses depend on decline from prior functioning and a coherent evolving profile, not simply low performance relative to norms.
supports: evolving pattern compatible with a disease network
challenges: stable lifelong weakness
performance normalises when mood, sleep or medication factors improve
no corroborated functional change over time
cases.nextStep: Integrate serial cognitive data with medical work-up, informant history and functional trajectory.
cases.caveat: Normal ageing, psychiatric illness, sensory impairment, medication effects and medical disease can mimic or amplify cognitive decline.

integratedCaseLab.title: Integrated healthy-to-pathology cases
integratedCaseLab.instruction: Work through localisation and assessment sequentially, then integrate supporting and conflicting evidence before committing to a formulation.

cases.label: Vascular network inefficiency
cases.vignette: An older adult with vascular risk factors shows slowed processing, reduced cognitive flexibility and variable attention, with relatively less prominent isolated storage failure.
clues: speed/executive efficiency is more affected than one focal cognitive module
daily function has changed gradually with possible stepwise periods
cases.hypothesisRationale: A speed/executive-dominant pattern in the context of vascular burden can fit distributed subcortical-white-matter network inefficiency, but profile alone cannot establish vascular causation.
cases.targetAssessment: Processing speed and executive control with vascular/functional context
assessmentOptions: Processing speed and executive control with vascular/functional context
cases.assessmentRationale: A broad battery should quantify speed, attention, set shifting, inhibition and memory while separating motor/visual slowing and integrating imaging, vascular history and everyday function.
supports: convergent slowing across low and higher executive-load tasks
executive inefficiency with retrieval benefiting from cueing
imaging and medical history show relevant vascular burden
challenges: isolated rapid forgetting with preserved speed/executive function
performance explained by depression, sleep, medication or sensory-motor factors
no evidence of vascular disease despite extensive workup
cases.synthesis: The profile can support a vascular-network hypothesis only when cognitive pattern, time course, medical risk and neuroimaging converge. Neuropsychology contributes pattern and functional impact, not vascular diagnosis by itself.
cases.nextStep: Integrate longitudinal history, neurological findings, imaging and modifiable vascular risks; repeat assessment when change over time is clinically important.
cases.caveat: Mixed pathologies are common in later life, and executive slowing is highly non-specific.

cases.label: Progressive memory syndrome
cases.vignette: A person has a progressive history of repeating questions and forgetting recent events despite cueing, with increasing impact on independent daily tasks.
clues: decline is progressive rather than abrupt
recent episodic learning is disproportionately affected
functional change is corroborated by an informant
cases.hypothesisRationale: Progressive rapid forgetting with impaired retention and functional decline raises a medial-temporal memory-system hypothesis, while aetiology still requires broader neurological and medical investigation.
cases.targetAssessment: Episodic learning, retention and recognition plus broader cognitive profile
assessmentOptions: Episodic learning, retention and recognition plus broader cognitive profile
cases.assessmentRationale: Learning curves, delayed recall, recognition, intrusion errors and comparison with language, executive and visuospatial domains help determine whether memory storage is disproportionately affected and whether the syndrome is focal or broader.
supports: poor delayed retention despite adequate initial exposure
limited benefit from recognition or cueing when true storage failure is present
progressive functional decline corroborated over time
challenges: memory normalises with cueing and slowed retrieval explains most difficulty
symptoms are static or abrupt rather than progressive
sleep, mood, medication or sensory factors better explain the pattern
cases.synthesis: A progressive amnestic pattern can identify the cognitive syndrome and guide differential diagnosis, but neuropsychological findings must be integrated with medical history, biomarkers/imaging when appropriate and longitudinal course.
cases.nextStep: Complete broader cognitive and functional assessment and coordinate neurological/medical workup appropriate to the clinical context.
cases.caveat: No single memory test score diagnoses a neurodegenerative disease, and mixed or atypical presentations are common.

sections.explainSimply: HEG uses near-infrared or thermal measures related to haemodynamic activity rather than electrical EEG rhythms.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Haemodynamic signals are slower and affected by systemic physiology, movement, scalp blood flow and device characteristics.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: HEG is a distinct modality and should not be presented as interchangeable with EEG neurofeedback. Evidence is limited and heterogeneous.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Choosing a camera lens: every method emphasises some information and introduces its own distortions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand heg neurofeedback to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Breathing and skin temperature can influence the signal.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using heg neurofeedback predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Breathing and skin temperature can influence the signal. Evidence classification: emerging; insufficient clinical evidence.

hypothalamus-atlas.title: Hypothalamus Atlas
hypothalamus-atlas.subtitle: Explore homeostatic nuclei coordinating endocrine, autonomic, circadian and motivated behaviour
hypothalamus-atlas.altText: Clinically labelled chalkboard-style anatomical illustration of the hypothalamus atlas, showing major subdivisions, connections and nearby landmarks.
learningObjectives: Locate the hypothalamus relative to the thalamus, third ventricle, optic chiasm and pituitary stalk.
Differentiate major hypothalamic nuclear zones and their homeostatic functions.
Relate hypothalamic pathways to endocrine, autonomic, circadian and behavioural presentations.

sections.explainSimply: The hypothalamus is a small control region beneath the thalamus. It monitors the body and coordinates temperature, thirst, hunger, hormones, sleep timing, stress responses and autonomic activity.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The hypothalamus translates internal bodily signals and context into endocrine, autonomic and motivated responses. It links interoception, emotion and behaviour through connections with the pituitary, brainstem, limbic system and cortex.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The hypothalamus forms the floor and inferolateral walls of the third ventricle. Its preoptic, anterior, tuberal and posterior regions contain nuclei with overlapping functions. The suprachiasmatic nucleus entrains circadian rhythms; paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei regulate neuroendocrine output; arcuate, lateral and ventromedial regions contribute to energy balance; mammillary bodies participate in memory circuitry; descending projections coordinate autonomic and defensive responses. Functional boundaries are networked rather than one-nucleus/one-function.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of it as the building-management system for the body: sensors report temperature, fuel, water and time, and the hypothalamus adjusts hormones, autonomic systems and behaviour to restore balance.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Sleep, appetite, stress reactivity, sexual behaviour, fatigue and autonomic symptoms can all involve hypothalamic systems. Understanding the circuitry improves biopsychosocial formulation without reducing symptoms to a single brain centre.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Lesions or dysfunction can disturb endocrine axes, circadian timing, temperature regulation, appetite, thirst, autonomic control and memory. Similar symptoms are common in non-hypothalamic conditions, so localisation requires medical assessment.
sections.clinicalPearl: The hypothalamus is tiny but strategically placed: a small lesion can affect several endocrine, autonomic and behavioural systems at once.
sections.clinicalExample: A suprasellar mass affecting the hypothalamic-pituitary region may present with sleep-wake disruption, endocrine change, altered appetite and reduced initiative rather than a single neat syndrome.
sections.limitationsCautions: Many human functional assignments derive from converging animal, lesion, imaging and stimulation studies. Poly-symptomatic presentations are expected because nuclei are small and densely interconnected.
sections.practicalExample: Use the hypothalamus atlas map to test whether a clinical pattern is anatomically coherent while considering network and medical alternatives.

sections.explainSimply: The insula is folded deep inside the lateral sulcus and helps integrate body signals with emotion, attention and action.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The insula supports interoception, salience detection and switching between internally and externally focused networks.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The insular cortex contains posterior-to-anterior gradients from primary interoceptive and somatosensory representations toward multimodal, affective and cognitive integration. It connects with thalamus, amygdala, cingulate, orbitofrontal cortex, striatum and brainstem autonomic centres.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A concealed control room that combines body telemetry with context before signalling what deserves attention.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Insular dysfunction can contribute to altered interoception, disgust processing, craving, pain, panic and salience attribution, but symptoms reflect network-level dysfunction rather than a single-region diagnosis.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Damage or dysregulation can disrupt salience network, interoception, autonomic regulation; presentations depend on laterality, extent and connected networks.
sections.clinicalPearl: Do not equate strong bodily awareness or anxiety with an “overactive insula”; infer mechanisms cautiously.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses the insula atlas map to test whether a patient’s pattern is anatomically coherent while considering broader network and medical explanations.
sections.limitationsCautions: Atlas localisation supports hypothesis generation, not diagnosis. Individual anatomy, distributed processing, compensation and comorbidity limit one-to-one structure–symptom claims.

integrated-whole-brain-explorer-and-caps.subtitle: Navigate the complete anatomy atlas and integrate structures, pathways, territories, networks and clinical patterns

learningObjectives: Navigate from a whole-brain overview to every completed Interactive Anatomy structure.

sections.explainSimply: The brain works as one connected system. Start with the whole-brain map, choose an anatomical family, add an overlay and open any detailed atlas structure.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Cognition, emotion and behaviour depend on interactions among cortical regions, deep nuclei, brainstem, cerebellum and connecting fibres. The capstone keeps localisation useful without reducing a person to one region.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Integrated localisation combines tissue compartment, laterality, tract course, network topology, vascular distribution and lesion mechanism. Cortico-subcortical loops, cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathways, ascending arousal systems and commissural, association and projection fibres make remote or distributed effects expected rather than exceptional.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A city map can show neighbourhoods, rail lines, utilities, traffic zones and disruptions on the same base map; each layer answers a different question, but no layer explains the city alone.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: The explorer links test findings and behaviour to plausible systems while preserving differential diagnosis, development, reserve, medications, fatigue, culture, psychosocial context and performance validity.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A focal cortical lesion may also disconnect fibres and depress remote nodes; a small deep lesion may affect compact motor, sensory and cognitive pathways; brainstem or cerebellar injury can alter cortical function through long loops; vascular and degenerative disease may cross several networks.
sections.clinicalPearl: Move through five questions: where is the change, which fibres pass there, which networks depend on them, which vascular or disease mechanism fits, and what evidence could disconfirm the hypothesis?
sections.practicalExample: For sudden aphasia and right face-arm weakness, compare hemispheres, open the cortical and white-matter domains, add vascular and lesion overlays, then navigate to arterial territories and lesion mapping. Treat the result as an urgent left-network vascular hypothesis requiring examination and imaging.
sections.limitationsCautions: This schematic explorer does not represent individual anatomy, imaging resolution, perfusion, temporal evolution or every connection. Overlay convergence strengthens a hypothesis but does not establish diagnosis, causality, prognosis or psychological meaning.

anatomy.position: Integrated whole-brain overview spanning bilateral cerebral cortex, deep nuclei, limbic and diencephalic structures, ventricles and meninges, brainstem, cerebellum, cranial nerves, white matter and cerebral vasculature.
anatomy.spatialRelationships: Cortical areas surround and connect with subcortical nuclei; projection, association and commissural fibres link hemispheres and levels; the brainstem joins cerebrum, cerebellum, spinal and cranial systems; arterial territories overlap and vary.
functions: navigate to every completed anatomy structure
inspect vascular, functional and lesion overlays
anatomy.bloodSupply: ACA, MCA and PCA cortical territories interact with deep perforators and vertebrobasilar, PICA, AICA and SCA territories. Watersheds and borders vary; venous, haemorrhagic and nonvascular mechanisms require different reasoning.
anatomy.lesionEffects: Clinical effects reflect local tissue injury, affected fibres, network disconnection, laterality, vascular distribution, diaschisis and time. Similar symptoms may arise from different sites, and similar lesions may produce different presentations.
neurologicalPresentations: altered arousal, memory or executive control
psychologicalPresentations: changes in attention, language, memory or social cognition
altered motivation, affect regulation or self-monitoring
variable disability shaped by reserve and environment
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: A whole-brain framework helps clinicians combine focal localisation with pathway, network and vascular reasoning, select detailed atlas views and state uncertainty without using anatomy as a stand-alone diagnosis.

explorerParts.short: Long tracts, nuclei and ascending regulation
explorerParts.detail: Navigate brainstem, reticular activating system and cranial nerves.
explorerParts.clinical: Crossed signs, arousal change and autonomic instability require urgent contextual assessment.

explorerParts.detail: Navigate hemispheres, vermis, deep nuclei and cerebellar peduncles.
explorerParts.clinical: Interpret cognitive-affective effects with concordant neurological and network evidence.

explorerParts.label: White matter and chemical pathways
explorerParts.detail: Navigate major association, commissural and projection pathways plus neurotransmitter systems.
explorerParts.clinical: Disconnection and neuromodulation can alter intact nodes across distance.

explorerParts.clinical: Territory borders vary; mechanism and time course remain essential.

explorerParts.label: Functional networks
explorerParts.detail: Navigate overlapping functional-network overlays across cortical and subcortical nodes.
explorerParts.clinical: Network membership is dynamic and does not assign one psychological function to one region.

explorerParts.label: Meninges and ventricular system
explorerParts.detail: Navigate meningeal layers and ventricular-CSF anatomy.
explorerParts.clinical: Mass effect, pressure, haemorrhage, inflammation and CSF obstruction can affect distant systems.

explorerParts.label: Lesion and symptom integration
explorerParts.detail: Navigate lesion mapping after comparing laterality and healthy-pathology patterns.
explorerParts.clinical: Use anatomy to rank and test hypotheses, never to reverse-infer a diagnosis or lived experience.

quiz.rationale: Broad orientation prevents premature localisation and supports structured comparison of sites, pathways, networks and mechanisms.

quiz.question: Why can a small subcortical lesion cause several deficits?
options: Compact nuclei and projection fibres serving several systems may lie close together
Every deep lesion affects the entire cortex equally
Symptoms depend only on lesion volume
quiz.rationale: Deep structures contain closely packed nuclei and fibres, so a small lesion may affect multiple connected functions.

quiz.question: What does convergence of a lesion overlay with a vascular territory and functional network establish?
options: A stronger anatomical hypothesis that still requires clinical and investigative confirmation
quiz.rationale: Converging layers improve coherence but cannot replace examination, imaging interpretation, course, differential diagnosis and context.

quiz.question: Which statement best integrates cerebellar and cortical anatomy?
options: Cerebellar effects can include coordination and connected cognitive-affective changes through cerebello-thalamo-cortical loops
The cerebellum controls cognition independently of the cerebrum
All affective symptoms localise to the vermis
Cortical function is unaffected by cerebellar connections
quiz.rationale: Cerebellar contributions are mediated through distributed loops; clinical interpretation requires neurological, temporal and network concordance.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the central mechanism in this concept?
reviewPrompts.answer: There is no single neural mechanism. Diverse aetiologies can alter synaptic development, excitation–inhibition balance, white-matter organisation, cortical maturation or metabolic function. Cognitive profiles are often uneven, and test performance is influenced by language, attention, motor demands, culture, opportunity and health. Adaptive functioning integrates real-world performance across conceptual, social and practical domains.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the most important clinical caution?
reviewPrompts.answer: IQ estimates capacity under test conditions; adaptive functioning determines how much support is needed in daily life.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What alternative explanations or red flags must be considered?
reviewPrompts.answer: Diagnostic overshadowing can cause pain, depression, psychosis, abuse or medical illness to be missed. Sudden functional decline is not explained by a lifelong developmental disability and needs assessment.

intergenerational-trauma.title: Intergenerational Trauma
intergenerational-trauma.subtitle: How adversity can affect later generations through multiple pathways
intergenerational-trauma.altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating intergenerational trauma across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.

sections.explainSimply: Trauma can influence families through caregiving, beliefs, stress exposure, social conditions and possibly biological pathways.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Intergenerational associations are supported across psychological, family and physiological outcomes, but human studies cannot cleanly separate caregiving, social and structural transmission from biological pathways. Epigenetic transmission remains plausible but unproven as a general causal explanation.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Human evidence is observational and vulnerable to shared-environment, historical, socioeconomic and measurement confounding. Epigenetic differences in descendants do not demonstrate inheritance of a trauma memory, nor do they establish an inevitable biological destiny.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of intergenerational trauma as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need intergenerational trauma to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Avoid deterministic claims that trauma is genetically “passed down.”
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use intergenerational trauma to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses intergenerational trauma to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Avoid deterministic claims that trauma is genetically or epigenetically “passed down.” Evidence classification: intergenerational associations are supported; specifically epigenetic transmission in humans remains limited and contested.

It is caused by poor motivation

quizBank.explanation: Dyslexia reflects persistent difficulty in reading processes despite adequate opportunity and is unrelated to low intelligence.

quizBank.question: A clinically useful assessment should primarily determine:

Whether the child tried hard enough
Whether one IQ score explains everything

quizBank.question: Which finding warrants broader investigation?
options: Sudden loss of previously established academic skills

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the core clinical distinction?
reviewPrompts.answer: A discrepancy between IQ and achievement is not required; the clinically important issue is persistent skill difficulty despite appropriate instruction.

Neuroimaging findings are group-level and heterogeneous rather than diagnostic biomarkers. Learning emerges through experience-dependent tuning of cortical systems that were not evolutionarily specialised for literacy or formal mathematics. Risk reflects polygenic liability, language exposure, instructional history and network efficiency. Intervention can alter activation patterns, but normalisation is neither necessary nor sufficient for functional improvement.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What red flags or alternatives matter?
reviewPrompts.answer: Do not infer laziness, low intelligence or poor parenting from slow academic progress. Sudden loss of established skills, seizures, neurological signs or broad regression require medical investigation.

sections.explainSimply: The learner receives information about a brain signal and gradually discovers ways to change the probability of reaching a target state.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Neurofeedback combines operant learning, skill acquisition, motivation, expectancy and repeated state practice. Non-specific factors can contribute to improvement.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Learning depends on contingency, salience, shaping, task difficulty, reinforcement timing and transfer beyond the training environment. Evidence of signal learning and evidence of symptom change are related but distinct.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A driving instructor who gives immediate dashboard feedback while the learner practises a controllable skill.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand learning theory to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A pleasant session is not proof that the intended neural feature was learned.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using learning theory predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: A pleasant session is not proof that the intended neural feature was learned. Evidence classification: established learning principles; theoretical neural transfer.

lesion-and-symptom-mapping.title: Lesion and Symptom Mapping
lesion-and-symptom-mapping.subtitle: Relate lesion location to pathways, networks, laterality, vascular territory and qualified symptom patterns
lesion-and-symptom-mapping.altText: Accessible chalkboard-style brain map showing bilateral cortical lesions, a deep subcortical lesion, an interrupted white-matter pathway, a brainstem lesion and a cerebellar lesion connected by uncertain routes to overlapping symptom-pattern cards and vascular territories.
learningObjectives: Relate lesion location, laterality and vascular territory to affected pathways and distributed networks.
Distinguish focal tissue injury, white-matter disconnection and distributed network dysfunction.
Compare qualified cortical, subcortical, white-matter, brainstem and cerebellar lesion patterns.
Use symptom patterns to generate differential hypotheses without assuming a one-lesion-one-symptom relationship.

sections.explainSimply: A lesion changes tissue at one place, but symptoms depend on what that place does, which pathways pass through it and how the rest of the network responds. The map supports hypotheses, not certainty.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Observed cognition, emotion and behaviour emerge from distributed systems. Laterality, disconnection, diaschisis, premorbid ability, reserve, development, time since injury and psychosocial context can all change the presentation expected from a lesion.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Lesion-symptom inference combines lesion topography and mechanism with tract anatomy, network membership, hemispheric specialisation, vascular territory, lesion load and temporal evolution. Focal cortical or nuclear damage may impair local computations; white-matter injury may disconnect intact nodes; distributed dysfunction may arise from multifocal disease, remote physiological depression or altered network dynamics. Many-to-many mapping is expected: one lesion can affect several functions and one symptom can arise from several sites or mechanisms.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A rail fault may damage one station, sever the track between intact stations or destabilise the timetable across the network; the same delayed journey can therefore have different causes.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Qualified mapping guides assessment selection, collateral questions, functional recommendations and rehabilitation while preventing biological overclaiming. Test profiles must be interpreted with neurological examination, imaging, course and performance validity.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A dominant perisylvian cortical lesion may impair language; a non-dominant temporoparietal lesion may contribute to neglect; a thalamic lesion may disturb arousal, sensation or cognition; arcuate or callosal injury may disconnect language or interhemispheric systems; a brainstem lesion may combine cranial-nerve and long-tract signs; a cerebellar lesion may impair coordination and cognitive-affective regulation. None of these patterns is obligatory or unique.
sections.clinicalPearl: Localise the pattern before naming the lesion: ask what is focal, what is disconnected, what is distributed, and which alternative mechanisms could produce the same findings.
sections.practicalExample: For sudden right face-arm weakness with aphasia, compare left and right mappings, inspect the lesion and symptom overlays, trace corticobulbar and language-network effects, then view the MCA territory. Treat the pattern as an urgent vascular hypothesis, not proof of one exact lesion.
sections.limitationsCautions: Atlas examples simplify variable anatomy and overlapping vascular borders. Lesion size, oedema, mass effect, seizure, perfusion, diaschisis, recovery, medications and comorbidity alter symptoms over time. Imaging may miss physiological dysfunction, and incidental lesions may be unrelated. Do not reverse-infer diagnosis, prognosis or psychological state from location alone.

anatomy.position: Whole-brain mapping across bilateral cortex, deep nuclei, long association and commissural white matter, brainstem and cerebellum.
anatomy.spatialRelationships: Each focal site is interpreted within adjacent tissue, traversing fibres, connected nodes, crossed or uncrossed pathways and arterial territories; remote effects may extend beyond the visible lesion.
inputs: premorbid function, reserve and contextual modifiers
connections: brainstem long tracts and cranial-nerve systems
outputs: explicit uncertainty and need for corroboration
functions: display associated neurological and psychological symptom patterns
trace an affected pathway or network
anatomy.bloodSupply: Cortical examples may follow ACA, MCA or PCA distributions; deep lesions may involve perforators; brainstem and cerebellar patterns may follow vertebrobasilar, PICA, AICA or SCA territories. Borders vary, and haemorrhage, venous disease and nonvascular lesions need different maps.
anatomy.lesionEffects: Focal lesions injure local tissue and nearby fibres; disconnection syndromes interrupt communication between relatively intact nodes; distributed dysfunction reflects multifocal injury, remote physiological effects or altered network dynamics. Effects vary with laterality, mechanism, extent and recovery and are never one-to-one.
neurologicalPresentations: altered arousal, memory or executive control
psychologicalPresentations: changes in attention, motivation or affect regulation
variable functional impact shaped by reserve and context
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Lesion-symptom mapping narrows anatomical and mechanistic hypotheses, guides urgent investigation and targeted assessment, and informs rehabilitation. It cannot independently establish aetiology, diagnosis, prognosis or an individual's psychological experience.

explorerParts.label: Whole-brain overview
explorerParts.detail: Compare focal tissue injury, tract disconnection and distributed network dysfunction across lesion sites, laterality and vascular patterns.
explorerParts.clinical: Begin with onset and the full sign pattern; use the map to rank hypotheses and alternatives, not to declare a diagnosis.

explorerParts.label: Left cortical lesion
explorerParts.short: Language-dominant patterns are common, not universal
explorerParts.detail: A left perisylvian or frontoparietal lesion may disrupt language, praxis, verbal working memory and contralateral sensorimotor systems through local and network effects.
explorerParts.clinical: Confirm language dominance and lesion extent. Aphasia patterns vary, and seizure, perfusion change or subcortical disconnection may mimic cortical injury.

explorerParts.label: Right cortical lesion
explorerParts.short: Spatial attention, prosody and contextual integration
explorerParts.detail: A right temporoparietal or frontal lesion may disturb spatial attention, prosody, visuospatial integration, awareness and contralateral sensorimotor systems.
explorerParts.clinical: Neglect is a distributed attention-network syndrome and is neither obligatory nor exclusive to one cortical site.

explorerParts.label: Subcortical lesion
explorerParts.short: Compact nuclei and fibres can yield mixed patterns
explorerParts.detail: Thalamic, basal-ganglia or internal-capsule lesions may combine sensory, motor, arousal, memory, language or executive changes because dense nuclei and pathways lie close together.
explorerParts.clinical: Small deep vascular lesions can have large effects, but exact syndromes vary with nucleus, fibre involvement, laterality and diaschisis.

explorerParts.label: White-matter disconnection
explorerParts.detail: Association, projection or commissural injury can disconnect language, attention, memory, visual-recognition or interhemispheric systems without destroying each connected cortical node.
explorerParts.clinical: Consider tract course and lesion load. Diffuse axonal injury and small-vessel disease often produce distributed rather than single-tract presentations.

explorerParts.label: Brainstem lesion
explorerParts.detail: Midbrain, pontine or medullary lesions may affect ipsilateral cranial-nerve systems alongside contralateral motor or sensory pathways, arousal circuits, autonomic control or cerebellar connections.
explorerParts.clinical: Crossed findings and abrupt onset can support brainstem vascular localisation, but urgent examination and imaging are required.

explorerParts.label: Cerebellar lesion
explorerParts.detail: Hemispheric or vermian lesions may cause ipsilateral limb dysmetria, gait or truncal ataxia, dysarthria and changes in timing; cognitive-affective effects reflect cerebello-cortical circuits.
explorerParts.clinical: Do not attribute psychiatric or cognitive symptoms to the cerebellum without a concordant neurological, temporal and network pattern.

explorerParts.label: Distributed network dysfunction
explorerParts.short: Symptoms without one sufficient focal site
explorerParts.detail: Multifocal disease, diaschisis, altered perfusion, seizure activity, metabolic disturbance or network degeneration can impair a system across connected regions.
explorerParts.clinical: An unremarkable focal scan does not exclude dysfunction; consider physiology, evolution, systemic factors and alternative diagnoses.

quiz.question: Why is one-lesion-one-symptom reasoning unsafe?
options: Symptoms and lesions have many-to-many relationships shaped by pathways, networks and individual context
Every symptom has one necessary cortical centre
quiz.rationale: A lesion can disturb several connected functions, while the same symptom can arise from different nodes, tracts or physiological mechanisms.

quiz.question: What best defines a disconnection syndrome?
options: Impaired communication between relatively intact nodes because connecting white matter is disrupted
Complete destruction of every node in a network
A symptom with no anatomical basis
quiz.rationale: Disconnection follows interruption of association, projection or commissural pathways rather than requiring destruction of all connected regions.

quiz.question: Which pattern most strongly supports a brainstem localisation?
options: An ipsilateral cranial-nerve deficit with a contralateral long-tract deficit
Isolated distress after an incidental scan finding
A single low memory score without neurological signs
quiz.rationale: Cranial-nerve nuclei or fascicles lie near ascending and descending long tracts, producing classic crossed patterns, although actual presentations vary.

quiz.question: What is the safest interpretation of a sudden aphasia with right face-arm weakness?
options: An urgent left-hemisphere vascular-network hypothesis requiring immediate stroke assessment
Proof of one exact cortical lesion
A psychological symptom unless imaging is positive
quiz.rationale: The pattern is compatible with a dominant left MCA-system event, but exact site and mechanism require urgent clinical and imaging confirmation.
