spacedRepetition.reviewPrompt: For one symptom pattern, compare a focal lesion, a white-matter disconnection and distributed network dysfunction, then name laterality, vascular and uncertainty checks.

accessibility.screenReaderSummary: Interactive lesion and symptom map with seven selectable lesion patterns, left-right comparison, pathway sequence, lesion, symptom, function and vascular overlays, uncertainty cautions and overview reset.

lesionLab.title: Symptom → localisation challenge
lesionLab.instruction: Start from the phenotype rather than the picture. Choose the best localisation hypothesis, then read the uncertainty statement.

cases.label: Language
cases.prompt: Sudden impaired naming and sentence formulation occur with right face-arm weakness. Spatial neglect is not prominent.
cases.rationale: A left hemispheric cortical or cortico-subcortical process is a strong localisation hypothesis when language change co-occurs with right-sided weakness.
cases.caveat: Language dominance varies, and subcortical or network disconnection can mimic a cortical syndrome. Acute focal deficits require emergency stroke assessment.

cases.label: Neglect
cases.prompt: A patient repeatedly ignores food and grooming on the left side and collides with objects on the left despite adequate primary vision for the task.
clues: Not explained by primary visual loss alone
cases.rationale: Right-lateralised attention-network injury, often involving temporoparietal and frontal systems, is a common substrate for left hemispatial neglect.
cases.caveat: Neglect is a distributed network syndrome and can occur with subcortical lesions or atypical laterality.

cases.label: Deep motor
cases.prompt: Abrupt dense contralateral weakness affects face, arm and leg with no clear aphasia, neglect or visual-field syndrome.
cases.rationale: A compact deep lesion affecting internal-capsular or neighbouring pathways can produce a dense motor syndrome with limited cortical features.
cases.caveat: This is a probabilistic localisation; brainstem and cortical lesions can sometimes produce similar patterns.

cases.label: Coordination
cases.prompt: Prominent limb dysmetria, gait ataxia and impaired timing occur without a primary weakness pattern.
cases.rationale: A cerebellar or cerebello-connected system is the leading localisation for dysmetria and gait ataxia when primary weakness does not explain the deficit.
cases.caveat: Vestibular, sensory and brainstem disorders can also cause imbalance or apparent ataxia and must be differentiated clinically.

cases.label: Network
cases.prompt: After diffuse white-matter injury, processing is slowed and executive coordination is inefficient across tasks without one clean focal cortical syndrome.
cases.rationale: Distributed white-matter disruption can reduce communication efficiency across multiple networks, producing slowed processing and broad executive inefficiency.
cases.caveat: Fatigue, mood, medication, sleep and many neurological conditions can also reduce processing efficiency; test interpretation requires context.

clinicalComparison.title: Compare intact systems with localisation hypotheses
clinicalComparison.instruction: Use the contrast to connect anatomy, mechanism and behaviour without treating any presentation as pathognomonic.

comparisons.label: Left cortical language network

healthy.label: Integrated language network
healthy.summary: Distributed dominant-hemisphere regions coordinate comprehension, formulation and speech with connected white matter.
healthy.mechanism: Cortical nodes and association pathways exchange phonological, semantic and motor information.
healthy.observable: Language is efficient enough for the person’s baseline and context.

pathology.label: Dominant cortical/network disruption
pathology.summary: Focal injury may disturb one or more language operations and their coordination.
pathology.mechanism: Local tissue dysfunction and disconnection can alter comprehension, naming, repetition, fluency or praxis.
pathology.observable: Aphasic features may occur alongside other focal signs depending on lesion extent.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: Use the pattern of spared and impaired language operations to generate a network-level localisation hypothesis.
comparisons.assessment: Sample spontaneous speech, naming, comprehension, repetition, reading and writing, then integrate neurological and imaging findings.
comparisons.caveat: Language dominance varies and aphasia profiles are not perfectly localising; perfusion, seizure and subcortical disconnection can mimic cortical patterns.

comparisons.label: White-matter disconnection

healthy.label: Connected network
healthy.summary: Relatively intact cortical nodes exchange information through association, projection and commissural fibres.
healthy.mechanism: Fast, coordinated transmission supports integration across specialised regions.
healthy.observable: Cross-region tasks are performed without a disconnection-specific bottleneck.

pathology.label: Disconnection
pathology.summary: Nodes may remain structurally intact while communication between them is impaired.
pathology.mechanism: Fibre injury interrupts transfer, timing or integration across a distributed system.
pathology.observable: Selective disconnection syndromes or broader slowing and inefficiency may occur.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: A deficit does not require destruction of the cortical regions that normally perform the computation; the connection itself may be the critical lesion.
comparisons.assessment: Look for dissociations and cross-modal or interhemispheric failures, then relate them to tract anatomy and lesion burden.
comparisons.caveat: Diffuse white-matter disease rarely respects a single tract and can produce distributed rather than textbook syndromes.

comparisons.label: Distributed network dysfunction

healthy.label: Coordinated distributed system
healthy.summary: Multiple nodes contribute to cognition through flexible, state-sensitive network interactions.
healthy.mechanism: Local computations are integrated through recurrent and long-range connectivity.
healthy.observable: Performance remains sufficiently stable across related tasks and everyday demands.

pathology.label: Network-level dysfunction
pathology.summary: Multifocal injury or remote physiological effects can degrade function beyond the visible lesion site.
pathology.mechanism: Diaschisis, altered connectivity, multifocal disease or reduced network efficiency can affect distant nodes.
pathology.observable: Broad or variable cognitive changes may exceed what a single focal lesion predicts.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: When the phenotype is wider than the visible lesion, consider network and remote effects before assuming poor effort or unrelated pathology.
comparisons.assessment: Integrate domain patterns, lesion burden, course, functional observations and performance validity.
comparisons.caveat: Network explanations remain hypotheses unless supported by convergent clinical and imaging evidence.

assessmentLab.title: Assessment-linked localisation reasoning
assessmentLab.instruction: Move from symptom pattern to testable functional hypotheses. Choose the domain that gives the highest-yield first evidence, then inspect what would support or challenge the localisation.

cases.label: Left cortical language
cases.prompt: After a left-hemisphere event, a patient has word-finding difficulty. Which assessment domain best tests whether this is a focal language syndrome rather than global cognitive slowing?
cases.rationale: Naming should be interpreted within fluency, comprehension, repetition, reading and writing so that the pattern—not one score—drives localisation.
challenges: uniform slowing across verbal and nonverbal tasks
severe hearing or speech-motor impairment
highly variable performance without language-specific pattern
cases.nextStep: Integrate language findings with neurological examination, imaging and premorbid language background.
cases.caveat: Language lateralisation varies, especially with handedness, multilingualism, development and prior neurological reorganisation.

cases.label: White-matter disconnection
cases.prompt: A patient has relatively preserved isolated skills but difficulty coordinating complex multi-step cognition after diffuse white-matter injury. What domain is most informative?
cases.rationale: Disconnection can disproportionately affect speed, coordination and executive integration while leaving some crystallised or focal skills relatively preserved.
observe: difference between simple and integrated tasks
supports: relative preservation of simpler component skills
challenges: isolated focal deficit without broader network inefficiency
performance explained by sedation, pain, sleep or mood
normal complex-task performance despite severe claimed disconnection
cases.nextStep: Control for motor speed, visual demands, fatigue and psychiatric factors before interpreting executive-speed findings as white-matter dysfunction.
cases.caveat: Diffuse slowing is non-specific and occurs in many neurological, psychiatric, sleep and medication-related states.

cases.label: Distributed network
cases.prompt: Symptoms span attention, memory, emotion regulation and social functioning without a clean focal neurological syndrome. What assessment strategy is best?
cases.rationale: Distributed hypotheses require convergence across domains, time course and functional contexts; a single test cannot establish network dysfunction.
supports: coherent cross-domain pattern matching known network demands
challenges: isolated low score without functional corroboration
inconsistent pattern dominated by situational factors
stronger alternative psychiatric, developmental or medical explanation
cases.nextStep: Formulate at the network and functional level and retain competing explanations until evidence converges.
cases.caveat: Network-level formulations are probabilistic. They should not be used to reverse-engineer a lesion or diagnosis from cognitive test scores alone.

integratedCaseLab.title: Integrated lesion-to-function cases
integratedCaseLab.instruction: Work through localisation and assessment sequentially, then integrate supporting and conflicting evidence before committing to a formulation.

cases.label: Dominant language network
cases.vignette: Following a focal neurological event, speech is effortful, naming is impaired and sentence repetition is poor, while alertness is intact.
clues: language change is acute and focal
motor speech versus language must be separated
laterality depends on individual language dominance
cases.hypothesisRationale: A multimodal language disturbance involving naming, connected speech and repetition is most coherently approached as a dominant perisylvian network problem, while still testing for dysarthria/apraxia and broader deficits.
cases.assessmentRationale: Sampling spontaneous speech, naming, comprehension, repetition, reading and writing establishes whether the deficit is genuinely language-based and which components are disproportionately affected.
supports: aphasic error types rather than pure motor weakness
imaging concordant with dominant language network
challenges: intact language with isolated dysarthria
global delirium or reduced arousal
hearing or motor impairment accounts for performance
cases.synthesis: The best working model is a dominant language-network disruption, but the examination must establish whether the observed communication difficulty is linguistic, motor-speech, attentional or mixed.
cases.nextStep: Map the full language profile and integrate neurological examination, imaging, handedness and premorbid language history.
cases.caveat: Language is distributed and individual dominance varies; a behavioural profile cannot specify a single cortical point lesion.

cases.label: Right attention network
cases.vignette: A patient repeatedly omits items on the left side of space, collides with objects on the left and is relatively unaware of the problem after a right-hemisphere event.
clues: asymmetry is spatial rather than simply visual acuity
cases.targetHypothesis: Right-lateralised attention-network disruption with left neglect
hypothesisOptions: Right-lateralised attention-network disruption with left neglect
cases.hypothesisRationale: Persistent left-sided omissions across tasks and everyday behaviour after right-hemisphere injury strongly support an attentional neglect hypothesis, although visual-field loss and motor/sensory deficits must be distinguished.
assessmentOptions: Fine motor speed in the right hand only
cases.assessmentRationale: Cancellation, line bisection, copying, visual search and functional observation across modalities help separate neglect from hemianopia, sensory loss and general inattention.
supports: left-sided omissions across more than one task
challenges: deficit maps exactly to a visual field without attentional bias
bilateral random omissions from reduced arousal
visual or motor limitations fully explain performance
alternatives: left-sided sensory extinction or motor impairment
cases.synthesis: The behavioural asymmetry supports a right attention-network hypothesis, but neglect is heterogeneous and should be characterised across reference frames and functional contexts.
cases.nextStep: Combine bedside neglect measures, visual-field examination and functional observation; assess safety implications.
cases.caveat: Neglect is a network syndrome and can vary markedly by task, modality and recovery stage.

limbic-system-atlas.title: Limbic System Atlas
limbic-system-atlas.subtitle: Explore memory, salience, motivation and emotion across connected circuits
limbic-system-atlas.altText: Medial brain and circuit diagram showing hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate cortex, fornix, mammillary bodies, hypothalamus and ventral striatum.
learningObjectives: Identify major limbic structures without treating the limbic system as a single emotion centre.
Trace hippocampal, amygdala, cingulate and hypothalamic connections.
Relate circuit disruption to memory, salience, motivation, autonomic response and psychopathology.

sections.explainSimply: The limbic system is a group of connected regions that help link memory, emotion, motivation, body state and action.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Limbic functions emerge from distributed loops involving cortex, subcortex, hypothalamus and brainstem; no single “emotional brain” explains complex behaviour.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Classical Papez circuitry overlaps with broader corticolimbic networks including amygdala, hippocampal formation, cingulate cortex, orbitomedial prefrontal cortex, ventral striatum, septal area and hypothalamus. These systems integrate context, salience, reinforcement and autonomic output.
sections.thinkOfItLike: It is a meaning-and-priority network that tags experiences, links them to memory and body state, and biases what the person does next.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Trauma, epilepsy, neurodegeneration and focal lesions may alter memory, threat appraisal, motivation or autonomic regulation through different limbic circuits.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Calling the amygdala the “fear centre” or the limbic system the “emotional brain” oversimplifies distributed, context-sensitive networks.
sections.clinicalPearl: Emotion and memory are not separate modules; they continually shape one another through recurrent corticolimbic loops.
sections.practicalExample: Bilateral hippocampal injury may profoundly impair new episodic learning while leaving immediate attention and procedural learning relatively intact.
sections.limitationsCautions: Psychiatric symptoms cannot be localised to one limbic structure; interpretation requires network, developmental and contextual formulation.

anatomy.label: Hippocampal formation
anatomy.function: Supports episodic encoding, context and spatial representation
anatomy.inputs: Entorhinal cortex and multimodal association input
anatomy.connections: Amygdala, cingulate, thalamic and prefrontal systems
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Bilateral dysfunction particularly affects new declarative learning.

anatomy.label: Amygdala complex
anatomy.function: Assigns salience and coordinates learned threat and value signals
anatomy.outputs: Hypothalamic, brainstem, striatal and cortical targets
anatomy.connections: Hippocampus, vmPFC, insula and salience network
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: It modulates salience and learning rather than generating one universal emotion.

anatomy.label: Cingulate cortex
anatomy.function: Integrates motivation, conflict, pain and internal state
anatomy.inputs: Prefrontal, thalamic, limbic and interoceptive input
anatomy.outputs: Motor, autonomic and cortical control systems
anatomy.connections: Papez circuit, salience and default-mode networks
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Anterior and posterior subdivisions have distinct network roles.

anatomy.label: Fornix–mammillary pathway
anatomy.function: Carries hippocampal output through diencephalic memory circuitry
anatomy.connections: Anterior thalamus and cingulate cortex
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Damage can impair recollection even when cortical memory regions remain structurally intact.

anatomy.label: Ventral striatum
anatomy.function: Integrates reward, motivation and action selection
anatomy.inputs: Prefrontal, hippocampal, amygdala and dopaminergic input
anatomy.connections: Mesolimbic and frontostriatal circuits
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Reward-related activation reflects learning and motivational value, not simple pleasure.

anatomy.label: Hypothalamus
anatomy.function: Coordinates endocrine, autonomic and homeostatic responses
anatomy.connections: Amygdala, hippocampus and prefrontal regulation
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Stress dysregulation, sleep and appetite disturbance
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Links subjective state with bodily regulation and action readiness.

lobes.title: The Cerebral Lobes
lobes.subtitle: Useful landmarks, not sealed compartments
learningObjectives: Use frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes as anatomical orientation landmarks.
Relate lobe-level specialisation to distributed network function.
Explain why lesion side, extent and connectivity matter more than a lobe label alone.

sections.explainSimply: The cortex is divided into lobes that help us describe where things happen. The borders are landmarks, not walls.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Frontal systems support executive control and action; parietal systems integrate sensory-spatial information; temporal systems support audition, memory and meaning; occipital cortex processes vision.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Each lobe contains multiple cytoarchitectonic and functional areas with extensive intra- and inter-lobar connectivity. Clinical effects depend on lesion side, extent, network position and premorbid organisation.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Suburbs in one city: each has a recognisable character, but roads and services cross every boundary.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Lobe-based summaries are useful for formulation but too coarse for definitive localisation or diagnosis.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Injury may produce executive dysfunction, neglect, aphasia, agnosia or visual field deficits depending on network involvement.
sections.clinicalPearl: Use lobes to orient yourself; use networks and behaviour to reason clinically.
sections.practicalExample: A right parietal lesion may disrupt spatial attention, but the severity and pattern depend on which cortical regions and connecting white-matter pathways are affected.
sections.limitationsCautions: Lobe-based localisation is deliberately coarse. Avoid statements such as “the frontal lobe controls personality” or “the temporal lobe is the memory centre.”

quizBank.question: Which lobe is most directly associated with primary visual processing?
quizBank.explanation: Primary visual cortex is located in the occipital lobe.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Explain the cerebral lobes in clinically useful terms.
reviewPrompts.answer: Frontal systems support executive control and action; parietal systems integrate sensory-spatial information; temporal systems support audition, memory and meaning; occipital cortex processes vision.

loreta-neurofeedback.title: LORETA Neurofeedback
loreta-neurofeedback.subtitle: Source-estimated training from scalp measurements
loreta-neurofeedback.altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating loreta neurofeedback within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain loreta neurofeedback without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in loreta neurofeedback.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to loreta neurofeedback.

sections.explainSimply: LORETA-based systems estimate distributed brain sources from scalp EEG and feed back a selected source metric.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Source localisation is an inverse solution constrained by model assumptions, electrode density, anatomy and noise. Spatial precision should not be overstated.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Training a source estimate adds modelling layers between measurement and reward. Reports should specify solver, regularisation, head model and target definition.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Choosing a camera lens: every method emphasises some information and introduces its own distortions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand loreta neurofeedback to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A colourful 3D source image is not direct intracranial measurement.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using loreta neurofeedback predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: A colourful 3D source image is not direct intracranial measurement. Evidence classification: emerging; insufficient clinical evidence.

major-white-matter-pathways-atlas.title: Major White-Matter Pathways Atlas
major-white-matter-pathways-atlas.subtitle: Explore projection, association, commissural and limbic fibre systems
major-white-matter-pathways-atlas.altText: Interactive chalkboard-style anatomical map of Major White-Matter Pathways Atlas with selectable regions and pathways.
learningObjectives: Identify the major components of the Major White-Matter Pathways Atlas.
Trace key inputs, outputs and connections in the Major White-Matter Pathways Atlas.
Interpret lesion patterns cautiously using distributed-network and clinical context.

sections.explainSimply: Explore projection, association, commissural and limbic fibre systems.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: White-matter integrity constrains processing speed, executive coordination and network synchronisation, but imaging associations are probabilistic and influenced by age, vascular health and methodology.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Location: Distributed myelinated fibre bundles connecting cortical, subcortical, brainstem and spinal regions across both hemispheres. Major subdivisions include corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus, arcuate fasciculus, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, cingulum bundle, fornix, optic radiations, corticospinal tract. Inputs include cortical neurons, thalamic nuclei, hippocampal formation, brainstem nuclei; outputs include contralateral cortex, ipsilateral cortical targets, subcortical nuclei, brainstem and spinal cord.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A dynamic transport and control map: the meaning of any node depends on the routes entering, leaving and bypassing it.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: White-matter integrity constrains processing speed, executive coordination and network synchronisation, but imaging associations are probabilistic and influenced by age, vascular health and methodology.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Disconnection may produce weakness, sensory loss, aphasia, neglect, visual-field deficits, amnesia or slowed processing depending on tract and network. Diffuse disease often causes broad inefficiency rather than a single focal syndrome.
sections.clinicalPearl: When grey matter looks intact but function is not, ask whether the pathway between nodes has failed.
sections.practicalExample: Select a region, trace its incoming and outgoing pathways, then compare healthy and lesion overlays before forming a clinical hypothesis.
sections.limitationsCautions: Named fasciculi overlap and tractography does not directly show axons or direction of information flow. Individual anatomy is variable and lesion-symptom mapping requires clinical correlation.

anatomy.position: Distributed myelinated fibre bundles connecting cortical, subcortical, brainstem and spinal regions across both hemispheres.
anatomy.spatialRelationships: Interpreted relative to connected cortical, subcortical and vascular structures; boundaries and laterality must be checked in the selected view.
anatomy.bloodSupply: Supplied by multiple cortical and deep perforating arterial territories; watershed zones and small-vessel disease can selectively affect long tracts.
anatomy.lesionEffects: Disconnection may produce weakness, sensory loss, aphasia, neglect, visual-field deficits, amnesia or slowed processing depending on tract and network. Diffuse disease often causes broad inefficiency rather than a single focal syndrome.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: White-matter integrity constrains processing speed, executive coordination and network synchronisation, but imaging associations are probabilistic and influenced by age, vascular health and methodology.

quiz.question: Which fibre class connects the two cerebral hemispheres?
quiz.rationale: Commissural pathways, especially the corpus callosum, connect homologous and heterologous regions across hemispheres.

quiz.question: A small lesion in the posterior limb of the internal capsule may cause dense weakness because:
options: Many descending motor fibres are tightly packed there
quiz.rationale: Compact organisation means a small lesion can affect many corticospinal fibres.

quiz.question: What is a key limitation of diffusion tractography?
options: It infers fibre orientation from water diffusion and can misrepresent crossing fibres
quiz.rationale: Tractography is an indirect reconstruction and is vulnerable to crossing-fibre and modelling limitations.

pathwayTrace.title: Trace disconnection through major white matter
pathwayTrace.instruction: Choose a pathway, follow the connected fibre route, then switch to Disrupted to predict the functional consequence before reading it.

pathways.label: Interhemispheric transfer
pathways.summary: Commissural fibres coordinate homologous and complementary processing across hemispheres.
pathways.healthy: Callosal fibres permit rapid exchange of sensory, motor and higher-order information between the hemispheres.
pathways.disrupted: Callosal injury can produce disconnection phenomena whose expression depends on lesion location, extent and task demands; findings are not reducible to a simple left-versus-right split.

pathways.label: Descending motor projection
pathways.summary: Motor commands converge through projection fibres on the way toward brainstem and spinal targets.
pathways.healthy: Distributed cortical motor output converges through corona radiata and the compact internal capsule before descending in the corticospinal system.
pathways.disrupted: A small lesion where fibres are densely packed, especially the internal capsule, can produce disproportionately broad contralateral weakness compared with a similarly sized lesion in more dispersed white matter.

pathways.label: Dorsal language pathway
pathways.summary: Frontotemporal-parietal association fibres support phonological and speech-motor integration within a distributed language network.
pathways.healthy: Dorsal association fibres support rapid coordination among temporal, parietal and frontal language-related regions.
pathways.disrupted: Damage may contribute to impaired repetition, phonological processing or speech-motor integration, but the phenotype depends on tract segment, cortical involvement and individual language organisation.

pathways.label: Ventral semantic pathway
pathways.summary: Long ventral association fibres link frontal, temporal and occipital regions for multimodal integration.
pathways.healthy: Ventral pathways support integration of semantic, visual and affective information across distant cortical regions.
pathways.disrupted: Disconnection can alter semantic access or frontotemporal integration, but tract-function mappings are probabilistic and overlap with neighbouring networks.

lesionLab.title: White-matter localisation challenge
lesionLab.instruction: Use the symptom pattern to choose the tract or fibre system that best explains the disconnection. Then inspect the caveat.

cases.label: Case 1
cases.prompt: A sudden small deep lesion is followed by marked contralateral face-arm-leg weakness with relatively little cortical cognitive change.
cases.rationale: The internal capsule contains densely packed descending and ascending fibres, so a small lesion can affect a large proportion of motor output.
cases.caveat: This is a localisation exercise, not a diagnosis. Vascular mechanism, sensory findings, imaging and examination determine the actual lesion.

cases.label: Case 2
cases.prompt: Speech remains fluent and comprehension is relatively preserved, but repetition and phonological sequencing are disproportionately impaired after a dominant-hemisphere lesion.
cases.rationale: The arcuate fasciculus is a major dorsal language pathway linking temporal-parietal and frontal language systems, although contemporary models treat repetition as network-based rather than a single-tract function.
cases.caveat: Cortical injury and other dorsal-stream fibres may produce similar findings; individual language organisation varies.

clinicalComparison.title: Compare intact tracts with disconnection
clinicalComparison.instruction: Use tract anatomy to connect network communication with the cognitive pattern expected when transmission is disrupted.

comparisons.label: Corpus callosum

healthy.label: Interhemispheric transfer
healthy.summary: Homologous and specialised cortical regions exchange information across the commissural system.
healthy.mechanism: Callosal fibres support integration and transfer between hemispheres.
healthy.observable: Tasks requiring cross-hemisphere integration proceed without a callosal bottleneck.

pathology.label: Callosal disconnection
pathology.summary: Interhemispheric information transfer may be selectively impaired despite relatively intact cortical nodes.
pathology.mechanism: Commissural fibre injury limits transfer of sensory, motor or cognitive information between hemispheres.
pathology.observable: Disconnection phenomena can emerge depending on lesion location and task demands.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: A callosal lesion is a network communication problem; behavioural effects depend on which fibres and cortical systems are disconnected.
comparisons.assessment: Use tasks that require interhemispheric transfer and interpret with lesion extent and handedness/lateralisation.
comparisons.caveat: Complete textbook disconnection syndromes are uncommon; partial lesions, compensation and bilateral representations alter presentation.

comparisons.label: Dorsal language pathway

healthy.label: Frontotemporal language integration
healthy.summary: Dorsal association fibres support communication among posterior and frontal language-related regions.
healthy.mechanism: Long-range white matter coordinates phonological and speech-production processes across nodes.
healthy.observable: Repetition and phonological integration are adequate for the person’s baseline.

pathology.label: Dorsal language disconnection
pathology.summary: Injury can disturb communication across otherwise viable language regions.
pathology.mechanism: Reduced tract integrity interrupts timing and transfer across the dorsal language system.
pathology.observable: Repetition or phonological language difficulties may be prominent within a broader variable profile.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: The tract model explains why language disturbance can reflect disconnection rather than destruction of one named language centre.
comparisons.assessment: Examine repetition, phonology, naming and fluency alongside comprehension and lesion anatomy.
comparisons.caveat: Language pathways are distributed and variable; arcuate injury is not synonymous with one fixed aphasia syndrome.

assessmentLab.title: Assessment-linked disconnection reasoning
assessmentLab.instruction: Test whether a suspected tract problem produces the functional disconnection pattern expected from that pathway.

cases.label: Callosal integration
cases.prompt: A patient shows unusual difficulty integrating information across the two hemispheres after a documented callosal lesion. What domain should be prioritised?
cases.rationale: A callosal hypothesis predicts difficulty transferring or integrating information across hemispheres rather than a global loss of knowledge.
observe: integration of lateralised visual or tactile information
discordance between intact unilateral skills and impaired transfer
supports: bimanual coordination difficulty disproportionate to unilateral motor skill
challenges: global cognitive impairment
peripheral sensory or motor deficits explaining the asymmetry
inconsistent lateralised effects
cases.nextStep: Interpret alongside handedness, lesion extent and other white-matter involvement.
cases.caveat: Real callosal lesions often coexist with neighbouring tissue damage; classic disconnection syndromes are uncommon in pure form.

cases.label: Language disconnection
cases.prompt: Speech is fluent and comprehension is relatively preserved, but repetition is disproportionately poor. Which domain is the best first target?
cases.rationale: A dorsal language-pathway hypothesis is strengthened by a disproportionate repetition/phonological working-memory problem relative to comprehension and semantic access.
observe: repetition across word and sentence length
challenges: equivalent impairment across comprehension, naming and repetition
hearing impairment or severe dysarthria accounting for performance
global attentional failure
cases.nextStep: Map the full language profile and imaging context rather than inferring an arcuate lesion from repetition alone.
cases.caveat: Language is network-based; dorsal stream disruption can involve multiple cortical and subcortical components beyond the arcuate fasciculus.

mechanisms-change-emdr.title: Mechanisms of Change
mechanisms-change-emdr.subtitle: A plural account of how EMDR may help
mechanisms-change-emdr.altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating mechanisms of change across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.

Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in mechanisms of change.

sections.explainSimply: EMDR may work through several overlapping processes rather than one special mechanism.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Exposure, dual attention, working-memory taxation, expectancy violation, reappraisal, therapeutic alliance and memory updating may all contribute.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Dismantling studies support a role for eye movements in reducing memory vividness, but comparative treatment efficacy does not establish a unique mechanism.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of mechanisms of change as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need mechanisms of change to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Avoid mechanism monoculture.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use mechanisms of change to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses mechanisms of change to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Avoid mechanism monoculture. Evidence classification: mixed, multi-mechanism evidence.

medication-considerations-neurofeedback.subtitle: Medication changes the state being measured and trained

learningObjectives: Explain medication considerations without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in medication considerations.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to medication considerations.

sections.explainSimply: Medication, caffeine, nicotine, alcohol and other substances can alter arousal and EEG features.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Record dose, timing, adherence and recent changes. Coordinate medication decisions with the prescriber rather than adjusting medication to improve a training metric.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Stable medication may improve interpretability. Abrupt changes can alter symptoms, sleep, seizure threshold and signal features.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A medication review: benefit, burden, adverse effects and alternatives must remain visible throughout care.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand medication considerations to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.

membrane.title: The Cell Membrane
membrane.subtitle: A selective electrical boundary
learningObjectives: Describe the phospholipid membrane as a selectively permeable electrical boundary.
Explain how pumps, channels and receptors maintain excitability.
Relate membrane targets to medication, electrolyte and channelopathy effects.

sections.explainSimply: The membrane is the cell’s flexible skin. It decides what can pass and helps keep the inside electrically different from the outside.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Ion gradients across the membrane make neural signalling possible. Channels, pumps and receptors translate chemical and electrical events into cellular responses.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The phospholipid bilayer is selectively permeable. Na+/K+-ATPase maintains sodium and potassium gradients, while ligand-gated and voltage-gated channels alter membrane conductance and excitability.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A secure border with gates, scanners and staff who use energy to keep traffic moving in the correct direction.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Many psychoactive medications act at membrane receptors, transporters or ion channels rather than changing brain structure directly.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Channelopathies, toxins and electrolyte disturbance can produce seizures, confusion, weakness or altered arousal.
sections.clinicalPearl: A neuron’s “decision” to fire emerges from thousands of membrane events summing over time and space.
sections.practicalExample: A change in extracellular potassium alters the electrochemical gradient across neuronal membranes. The resulting shift in excitability can affect consciousness, muscle function and seizure risk.
sections.limitationsCautions: Membrane mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient explanations for complex symptoms. The same channel or receptor can have different effects across cell types and circuits.

quizBank.question: What maintains the major sodium and potassium gradients?
quizBank.explanation: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to preserve the gradients that support resting potential and action potentials.

meninges-atlas.title: Meninges Atlas
meninges-atlas.subtitle: Explore protective layers, dural reflections, venous sinuses and CSF spaces
meninges-atlas.altText: Layered sagittal brain illustration showing dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater, subarachnoid space, dural reflections and venous sinuses.
learningObjectives: Identify dura, arachnoid, pia and the clinically relevant meningeal spaces.
Relate dural reflections and venous sinuses to intracranial compartmentalisation and drainage.
Differentiate epidural, subdural and subarachnoid pathology by anatomy and mechanism.

sections.explainSimply: The meninges are three protective coverings wrapped around the brain and spinal cord. Their layers create spaces for blood vessels and cerebrospinal fluid.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Meningeal anatomy matters because haemorrhage, infection, pressure shifts and pain-sensitive structures can alter cognition, behaviour and consciousness even when brain tissue is initially intact.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The pachymeninx is dura mater; the leptomeninges are arachnoid and pia. Dural border cells permit subdural separation, while the subarachnoid space contains CSF, arteries and bridging veins. Dural folds partition the cranial cavity and house venous sinuses.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of three nested protective sleeves: a tough outer shell, a web-like middle membrane and a delicate inner film that follows every contour.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Headache, altered consciousness and focal deficits may arise from meningeal haemorrhage, inflammation or pressure effects; localisation requires attention to layer and compartment.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Treating all extra-axial bleeding as equivalent obscures different vessels, time courses and emergency risks.
sections.clinicalPearl: The “subdural space” is usually a potential space created by tissue separation, not a pre-existing open cavity.
sections.practicalExample: An older adult with falls and gradually worsening confusion may have a chronic subdural haematoma from torn bridging veins.
sections.limitationsCautions: This atlas supports anatomical learning only; suspected meningitis or intracranial haemorrhage requires urgent medical assessment.

anatomy.label: Dura mater
anatomy.function: Tough outer meningeal layer and pain-sensitive cranial covering
anatomy.inputs: Periosteal attachment and meningeal vascular innervation
anatomy.outputs: Dural folds and venous sinus walls
anatomy.connections: Dural venous sinuses and cranial periosteum
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Helps distinguish arterial epidural bleeding and dural pain sources.

anatomy.label: Arachnoid mater
anatomy.function: Barrier membrane enclosing the CSF-filled subarachnoid space
anatomy.inputs: Interfaces with dura and arachnoid trabeculae
anatomy.connections: CSF pathways and pia via trabeculae
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Its barrier and granulations are central to CSF containment and resorption.

anatomy.label: Pia mater
anatomy.function: Delicate vascular membrane closely investing brain surface
anatomy.connections: Glia limitans and superficial vasculature
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Inflammation can track along vessels and cortical surfaces.

anatomy.label: Subarachnoid space
anatomy.function: Contains CSF, major arteries, veins and cisterns
anatomy.connections: Basal cisterns, cortical sulci and spinal space
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Blood or infection in this space can distribute widely and irritate meninges.

anatomy.label: Dural venous sinuses
anatomy.function: Drain cerebral veins and receive CSF
anatomy.connections: Falx, tentorium and skull base channels
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Venous outflow obstruction may cause headache, seizures and raised intracranial pressure.

accessibility.altText: Layered sagittal brain illustration showing dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater, subarachnoid space, dural reflections and venous sinuses.
accessibility.screenReaderSummary: The meninges are three protective coverings wrapped around the brain and spinal cord. Their layers create spaces for blood vessels and cerebrospinal fluid.

learningObjectives: Identify the major components of the Meninges.
Explain how the Meninges contributes to sensation, regulation or behaviour.
Connect Meninges function with clinically relevant symptoms.
Use lesion patterns and phenomenology cautiously rather than relying on one-to-one explanations.

anatomy.label: Dura mater
anatomy.detail: Dense connective tissue stabilises the cranial contents and forms venous sinuses.
anatomy.clinical: Dural irritation can generate pain; tears may cause CSF leak.

anatomy.label: Arachnoid mater
anatomy.detail: Bridges over sulci and encloses the CSF-filled subarachnoid space.
anatomy.clinical: Blood in this space produces subarachnoid haemorrhage.

anatomy.label: Subarachnoid space
anatomy.detail: Provides buoyancy and a route for cerebral arteries.
anatomy.clinical: Infection or haemorrhage here can irritate the meninges.

anatomy.label: Pia mater
anatomy.detail: Closely follows gyri, sulci and the spinal cord surface.
anatomy.clinical: Inflammation often involves pia and arachnoid together.

anatomy.label: Dural venous sinuses
anatomy.detail: Receive cerebral venous blood and CSF resorption.
anatomy.clinical: Thrombosis can cause headache, seizures and focal deficits.

learningObjectives: Identify the soma, motile processes, phagocytic machinery, purinergic receptors and complement-related signalling used by microglia.
Explain how microglia survey tissue, respond to damage signals and clear debris while preserving viable neural tissue.
Describe microglial roles in development, synaptic remodelling and homeostasis without reducing them to a simple resting-versus-activated model.
Apply microglial principles cautiously to neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative and psychiatric research without treating inflammation as a universal explanation.

anatomy.label: Microglial soma
anatomy.detail: The soma contains the nucleus and organelles that coordinate sensing, movement, cytokine production and phagocytosis. In healthy tissue, the soma is relatively small while its processes extend widely through the local environment.
anatomy.clinical: Microglia can alter gene expression and morphology rapidly. A change in shape is informative, but it does not by itself reveal whether the response is protective, reparative or harmful.

anatomy.label: Surveying processes
anatomy.detail: Fine processes continuously extend and retract to sample the surrounding extracellular space, contact synapses and detect local changes. The cell body may remain stationary while the processes are highly dynamic.
anatomy.clinical: The older label 'resting microglia' is misleading. Homeostatic microglia are active sentinels even when there is no overt injury.

anatomy.label: Damage-signal receptors
anatomy.detail: Microglia respond to extracellular ATP, altered lipids, complement fragments and other danger-associated signals through receptor systems including purinergic receptors. These cues guide process movement and local response intensity.
anatomy.clinical: Microglial responses are context-dependent. The same signalling pathway may support repair in one setting and contribute to tissue injury in another.

anatomy.label: Phagocytic compartment
anatomy.detail: Microglia can engulf apoptotic cells, damaged myelin, pathogens and selected synaptic elements. Internalised material is processed through phagosomes and lysosomes.
anatomy.clinical: Effective clearance can limit secondary injury. Excessive or poorly targeted engulfment may remove viable synapses or prolong dysfunction.

anatomy.label: Complement tagging
anatomy.detail: Complement proteins can label cellular material or synaptic elements for removal. During development, complement-related signalling helps refine circuits by supporting activity-dependent synaptic elimination.
anatomy.clinical: Complement-mediated pruning is well established in developmental animal models, but translating this directly into a diagnosis for an individual patient would be an overreach.

anatomy.label: Synaptic contact
anatomy.detail: Microglial processes contact synaptic structures and can influence synapse formation, maintenance and elimination. Their contribution varies across developmental stage, brain region and physiological context.
anatomy.clinical: Microglia contribute to plasticity, but behaviour still emerges from distributed cellular, circuit, endocrine and environmental systems.

anatomy.label: Signalling molecules
anatomy.detail: Microglia release cytokines, chemokines, trophic factors and reactive molecules that influence neurons, astrocytes, vascular cells and other immune cells. The effect depends on dose, timing, combination and tissue state.
anatomy.clinical: Inflammation is not synonymous with damage. Short, proportionate immune signalling can be adaptive; persistent dysregulation can become maladaptive.

interaction.instruction: Select a microglial system, then run the surveillance cycle to follow tissue sensing, target recognition, engulfment and resolution.
surveillanceSteps: Motile processes continuously sample the local neural environment.

Tagged debris is engulfed into a phagosome and broken down through lysosomal pathways.

quizBank.question: Which statement about microglial activation states is most accurate?

quizBank.explanation: Modern microglial biology emphasises diverse, context-sensitive states rather than a single binary resting-versus-activated model.

options: Inflammation may matter, but source, timing and evidence must be specified
All psychiatric symptoms are caused by cytokines

quizBank.explanation: Neuroimmune findings require careful interpretation. Inflammation is a process, not a stand-alone explanation for every symptom.

quizBank.question: Migraine aura is most closely linked to:
quizBank.explanation: A slowly propagating wave of depolarisation is the leading mechanism for aura.

quizBank.explanation: CGRP is a key mediator and treatment target in migraine.

quizBank.question: Which headache presentation is most urgent?
options: A familiar migraine relieved by the usual plan
Mild tension after a long day
quizBank.explanation: Thunderclap headache can indicate subarachnoid haemorrhage or other acute pathology.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the central mechanism in this concept?
reviewPrompts.answer: Cortical spreading depolarisation is strongly linked to aura, while trigeminal afferents and calcitonin gene-related peptide contribute to meningeal nociceptive signalling. Hypothalamic and brainstem changes may precede pain, consistent with a cyclic state disorder rather than a purely vascular event. Central sensitisation can produce allodynia and chronification. Genetic susceptibility, sleep, hormones, sensory load and learning history influence threshold.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the most important clinical caution?
reviewPrompts.answer: Migraine is a disorder of brain state regulation and sensory processing, not simply dilated blood vessels.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What alternative explanations or red flags must be considered?
reviewPrompts.answer: A sudden thunderclap headache, new focal deficit, fever with neck stiffness, pregnancy-related severe headache or a major change in pattern requires urgent medical assessment.

moral-injury.title: Moral Injury
moral-injury.subtitle: Psychological impact of violating or witnessing deeply held values
moral-injury.altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating moral injury across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain moral injury in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in moral injury.

sections.explainSimply: Moral injury centres on guilt, shame, betrayal, anger and loss of meaning after morally injurious events.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: It can coexist with PTSD but is not reducible to fear circuitry or currently a standalone formal diagnosis.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Mechanistic research is early; social, spiritual and cultural dimensions are central and cannot be replaced by neurobiology.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of moral injury as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need moral injury to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not medicalise ethical conflict or bypass accountability and repair.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use moral injury to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses moral injury to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not medicalise ethical conflict or bypass accountability and repair. Evidence classification: emerging construct.

learningObjectives: Trace voluntary movement from cortical planning to spinal execution.
Distinguish basal-ganglia action selection from cerebellar error correction.
Relate upper- and lower-motor-neuron signs to pathway level.
Avoid treating all reduced movement as weakness.

anatomy.label: Premotor and supplementary cortex
anatomy.detail: These frontal regions prepare movements using internal goals and external cues.
anatomy.clinical: Disruption may cause impaired sequencing, initiation or apraxic errors.

anatomy.label: Primary motor cortex
anatomy.detail: M1 contributes fractionated voluntary control through corticospinal and corticobulbar projections.
anatomy.clinical: Focal injury commonly produces contralateral weakness and loss of fine control.

anatomy.label: Basal ganglia
anatomy.detail: Parallel loops facilitate useful actions while suppressing competitors.
anatomy.clinical: Circuit imbalance contributes to bradykinesia, rigidity, dystonia and hyperkinesia.

anatomy.label: Cerebellum
anatomy.detail: Cerebellar circuits compare intended and actual outcomes to refine timing and accuracy.
anatomy.clinical: Lesions cause ipsilateral ataxia, dysmetria and impaired motor learning.

anatomy.label: Brainstem and spinal cord
anatomy.detail: Descending pathways converge on interneurons and lower motor neurons.
anatomy.clinical: Damage may produce weakness, altered tone, abnormal reflexes or patterned posturing.

stages.label: Plan

stages.label: Select

stages.label: Learn

quizBank.explanation: Basal-ganglia loops help select and scale actions while suppressing competitors.

quizBank.question: An upper-motor-neuron lesion commonly produces:

quizBank.explanation: Loss of descending control can produce weakness, hyperreflexia and spasticity.

quizBank.question: Apraxia refers to:
options: Impaired learned action despite sufficient basic strength
quizBank.explanation: Apraxia is a disorder of learned purposeful action not explained by elementary weakness alone.

anatomy.label: Oligodendrocyte precursor
anatomy.short: Proliferative cell capable of becoming myelinating glia
anatomy.detail: OPCs remain abundant and responsive across development.
anatomy.clinical: Their proliferation and differentiation are sensitive to injury and activity.

anatomy.label: Differentiation
anatomy.detail: Maturing cells extend processes and select axons for wrapping.
anatomy.clinical: Failure of differentiation can limit repair even when precursors are present.

anatomy.label: Internode
anatomy.detail: Each sheath forms a discrete internode around one axon segment.
anatomy.clinical: Internode geometry influences conduction velocity and timing.

anatomy.label: Node of Ranvier
anatomy.detail: Voltage-gated sodium channels cluster at nodes between sheaths.
anatomy.clinical: Disrupted nodal organisation can impair conduction without complete axon loss.

anatomy.label: White-matter tract
anatomy.detail: Increasing myelination changes diffusion, timing and network efficiency.
anatomy.clinical: White-matter measures reflect multiple tissue properties and are not direct readouts of one psychological function.

sections.explainSimply: EMDR is a structured psychotherapy that uses trauma recall with bilateral stimulation within a broader eight-phase protocol.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Clinical efficacy for PTSD is supported by guidelines, while proposed mechanisms include working-memory taxation, orienting responses, extinction and memory updating.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Neuroimaging studies report changes after treatment, but small samples and non-specific therapy effects limit causal conclusions.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of neurobiology of emdr as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need neurobiology of emdr to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not present one neural mechanism as proven.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use neurobiology of emdr to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses neurobiology of emdr to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not present one neural mechanism as proven. Evidence classification: established efficacy for PTSD; mechanisms mixed.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the central mechanism in this concept?
reviewPrompts.answer: Protein misfolding, impaired proteostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, synaptic failure and selective cellular vulnerability interact differently across diseases. Amyloid-β and tau are central to Alzheimer pathophysiology; α-synuclein to Parkinson/Lewy body disorders; tau or TDP-43 to many frontotemporal degenerations. Biomarkers support diagnosis but must be interpreted within phenotype and stage.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the most important clinical caution?
reviewPrompts.answer: “Dementia” describes functional impact, not one disease. Diagnose the syndrome, consider the cause, and always establish time course.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What alternative explanations or red flags must be considered?
reviewPrompts.answer: Progressive memory loss, visuospatial errors, fluctuations, hallucinations, parkinsonism, disinhibition, language decline or loss of daily function may signal disease-specific syndromes. Sudden decline is not typical degeneration and requires urgent evaluation for delirium, stroke or other acute causes.

learningObjectives: Identify the dendrites, soma, axon hillock, axon, myelin, nodes of Ranvier and presynaptic terminals.
Explain how a neuron transforms distributed synaptic input into an all-or-none axonal output.
Distinguish neuronal signalling from the broader activity of neural networks.
Apply neuronal principles to psychological learning, medication effects and clinical symptoms without reducing complex behaviour to a single cell.

anatomy.label: Dendrites
anatomy.detail: Dendrites receive thousands of excitatory, inhibitory and modulatory synaptic inputs. Their branching geometry and receptor distribution shape how strongly each input influences the soma.
anatomy.clinical: Changes in dendritic spines are one cellular correlate of learning, stress exposure and synaptic plasticity.

anatomy.label: Soma
anatomy.detail: The soma contains the nucleus and most organelles. It maintains the neuron and integrates currents arriving from dendrites before they reach the axon hillock.
anatomy.clinical: Neurons have high energy demands; hypoxia, mitochondrial dysfunction and excitotoxicity can rapidly compromise their function.

anatomy.label: Axon hillock
anatomy.detail: The axon initial segment contains a high density of voltage-gated sodium channels. When summed membrane depolarisation reaches threshold, an action potential begins.
anatomy.clinical: The firing threshold is dynamic and is shaped by recent activity, neuromodulators and inhibitory control.

anatomy.label: Axon
anatomy.detail: The axon conducts action potentials away from the soma. Axonal diameter, myelination and ion-channel distribution influence conduction speed.
anatomy.clinical: Diffuse axonal injury can disrupt cognition and arousal even when conventional structural imaging appears relatively subtle.

anatomy.label: Myelin
anatomy.detail: Myelin limits current leakage and enables rapid saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier. In the central nervous system it is produced by oligodendrocytes.
anatomy.clinical: Demyelination slows or blocks transmission and can produce sensory, motor and cognitive symptoms depending on the affected pathways.

anatomy.label: Nodes of Ranvier
anatomy.detail: Nodes are short unmyelinated axonal segments rich in voltage-gated channels. The action potential is actively regenerated at each node.
anatomy.clinical: Saltatory conduction is not a literal leap through empty space; local current spreads under myelin and triggers the next node.

anatomy.label: Presynaptic terminals
anatomy.detail: When an action potential reaches a terminal, calcium entry triggers synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release into the synaptic cleft.
anatomy.clinical: Many medications and toxins alter release, receptor binding or transmitter clearance rather than changing neuronal anatomy.

quizBank.question: Why does myelin increase conduction speed?
options: It reduces current leakage and supports saltatory conduction
It makes neurotransmitters move faster through blood
It increases the size of the nucleus
It removes the need for ion channels
quizBank.explanation: Myelin electrically insulates axonal segments, allowing current to spread efficiently to the next node of Ranvier.

quizBank.question: Which event directly triggers neurotransmitter release from a presynaptic terminal?
quizBank.explanation: Action-potential arrival opens voltage-gated calcium channels; calcium then triggers vesicle fusion.

reviewPrompts.prompt: Why is a neuron more than a passive wire?
reviewPrompts.answer: It integrates inputs, changes excitability, modifies synaptic strength and participates differently depending on network state and experience.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the clinical danger of treating one neurotransmitter or neuron as the explanation for behaviour?
reviewPrompts.answer: Psychological functions emerge from interacting circuits, physiology, learning and context; single-cell explanations are usually reductionistic.

learningObjectives: Differentiate synaptic, structural, intrinsic and network plasticity.
Explain LTP, LTD and homeostatic plasticity at a conceptual level.
Apply plasticity principles to psychotherapy and rehabilitation.
Recognise how plasticity can maintain both adaptive and maladaptive patterns.

anatomy.label: Long-term potentiation
anatomy.detail: Repeated coordinated activity can strengthen synaptic responses through NMDA-dependent calcium signalling, AMPA-receptor trafficking and downstream molecular change.
anatomy.clinical: LTP is one mechanism relevant to learning, but it is not a complete explanation of memory.

anatomy.label: Long-term depression
anatomy.detail: Different activity patterns can reduce synaptic strength, supporting refinement, forgetting and flexible updating.
anatomy.clinical: Weakening old predictions may be as important as strengthening new ones in therapy.

anatomy.label: Structural plasticity
anatomy.detail: Dendritic spines, axonal boutons and myelin can change with experience over hours to months.
anatomy.clinical: Structural change is constrained by age, health, stress, sleep and repeated practice.

anatomy.label: Homeostatic plasticity
anatomy.detail: Cells adjust excitability and receptor expression to prevent activity from drifting too high or too low.
anatomy.clinical: Homeostatic compensation can blunt treatment effects or stabilise networks after perturbation.

anatomy.label: Systems consolidation
anatomy.detail: Over time, memories become represented through changing interactions among hippocampal and cortical systems.
anatomy.clinical: Sleep and repeated retrieval support consolidation and integration.

quizBank.explanation: Plasticity remains possible across life but is not unconstrained.

sections.explainSimply: Trace major monoaminergic, cholinergic and amino-acid signalling systems.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Neurotransmitters modulate distributed circuits. Terms such as “chemical imbalance” are clinically misleading when used as simple explanations for complex mental disorders.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Location: Small brainstem, midbrain, hypothalamic and basal-forebrain nuclei project broadly, while glutamate and GABA operate throughout local and long-range circuits. Major subdivisions include locus coeruleus, dorsal and median raphe, ventral tegmental area, substantia nigra pars compacta, basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei, tuberomammillary nucleus, cortical glutamate systems, GABA interneuron networks. Inputs include prefrontal cortex, hypothalamus, brainstem sensory systems, limbic structures; outputs include cerebral cortex, hippocampus, striatum, thalamus, spinal and autonomic systems.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A dynamic transport and control map: the meaning of any node depends on the routes entering, leaving and bypassing it.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Neurotransmitters modulate distributed circuits. Terms such as “chemical imbalance” are clinically misleading when used as simple explanations for complex mental disorders.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Focal or degenerative disruption may alter arousal, movement, memory, autonomic regulation or affect, but behavioural effects emerge from receptor distribution and network state rather than transmitter level alone.
sections.clinicalPearl: A neurotransmitter is not an emotion: it changes the gain and plasticity of circuits that generate behaviour in context.
sections.practicalExample: Select a region, trace its incoming and outgoing pathways, then compare healthy and lesion overlays before forming a clinical hypothesis.
sections.limitationsCautions: Pathway maps simplify co-transmission, receptor diversity, volume transmission and feedback. Medication effects cannot be inferred from a single pathway diagram.

learningObjectives: Differentiate fast transmitters from neuromodulators.
Explain why receptor subtype determines effect.

anatomy.label: Glutamate
anatomy.detail: Glutamate activates AMPA, NMDA and metabotropic receptors across cortical and subcortical circuits.
anatomy.clinical: Excessive glutamatergic activation can contribute to excitotoxicity, while NMDA-dependent signalling supports plasticity.

anatomy.label: GABA
anatomy.detail: GABA-A receptors usually increase chloride conductance; GABA-B receptors act through slower G-protein mechanisms.
anatomy.clinical: Reduced inhibitory control can increase network instability and seizure susceptibility.

anatomy.label: Dopamine
anatomy.detail: Dopamine modulates prediction error, motivation, movement and working-memory gating through several receptor families and pathways.
anatomy.clinical: Effects differ markedly across nigrostriatal, mesolimbic, mesocortical and tuberoinfundibular pathways.

anatomy.label: Serotonin
anatomy.detail: Serotonin acts through many receptor subtypes to influence mood, sleep, appetite, pain and behavioural adaptation.
anatomy.clinical: SSRIs change transporter function quickly, but therapeutic adaptation usually unfolds over weeks.

anatomy.label: Noradrenaline
anatomy.detail: Locus-coeruleus projections modulate vigilance, signal-to-noise ratio and responses to uncertainty.
anatomy.clinical: Both insufficient and excessive arousal can impair executive performance.

anatomy.label: Acetylcholine
anatomy.detail: Basal forebrain acetylcholine supports attention and cortical plasticity; other cholinergic systems regulate motor and autonomic function.
anatomy.clinical: Cholinergic loss is prominent in Alzheimer disease, while anticholinergic burden can impair cognition.

quizBank.question: Why can the same neurotransmitter have different effects?

Its molecules change colour in each brain region
quizBank.explanation: Receptor coupling and circuit context determine functional effect.

quizBank.question: Which pair dominates fast cortical excitation and inhibition?

quizBank.question: Dopamine is best understood as:
options: A context-dependent modulator of learning, salience and action
The single chemical cause of pleasure
A hormone that never acts in brain

quizBank.question: Why do SSRI clinical effects usually lag behind transporter blockade?

Serotonin must physically grow new neurons first
The blood–brain barrier opens only after weeks
quizBank.explanation: Immediate transporter effects lead to slower adaptive changes across systems.

quizBank.explanation: Acetylcholine supports attention and memory, especially in basal forebrain systems.

learningObjectives: Identify the oligodendrocyte soma, branching processes, compact myelin, internodes, paranodes and nodes of Ranvier.
Explain how myelin changes membrane capacitance and resistance to support rapid saltatory conduction.
Describe how oligodendrocytes provide metabolic support to axons in addition to electrical insulation.
Relate demyelination, remyelination and white-matter disruption to processing speed, fatigue and distributed cognitive function without over-localising symptoms.

anatomy.label: Oligodendrocyte soma
anatomy.detail: The soma contains the nucleus and biosynthetic machinery that produces the large quantities of lipid and protein required for myelin. Mature oligodendrocytes extend several processes from one compact cell body.
anatomy.clinical: Because myelin production is metabolically demanding, oligodendrocytes are vulnerable to oxidative stress, inflammation and disrupted energy supply.

anatomy.label: Myelinating processes
anatomy.detail: Branching processes contact multiple axons and form separate myelin internodes. Unlike a peripheral Schwann cell, one oligodendrocyte can myelinate portions of several central nervous system axons.
anatomy.clinical: Damage to one oligodendrocyte can therefore affect conduction across more than one axonal segment or pathway.

anatomy.label: Compact myelin
anatomy.detail: Myelin is formed when oligodendrocyte membrane wraps repeatedly around an axon and compacts into a multilamellar sheath. It raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance across the internode.
anatomy.clinical: Myelin is not simply plastic coating. It is living membrane that must be maintained and coordinated with the axon it surrounds.

anatomy.label: Internode
anatomy.detail: An internode is the myelinated length between two nodes of Ranvier. Internode length and sheath thickness influence conduction speed and timing across a pathway.
anatomy.clinical: Distributed cognition depends on signals arriving within useful temporal windows; altered white-matter timing can disrupt coordination even when cortical regions remain structurally intact.

anatomy.label: Node of Ranvier
anatomy.detail: Nodes are short unmyelinated gaps enriched in voltage-gated sodium channels. Depolarising current travels rapidly beneath myelin, while the full action potential is regenerated at successive nodes.
anatomy.clinical: Demyelination exposes axonal membrane and redistributes current, slowing conduction or producing conduction block.

anatomy.label: Paranodal junction
anatomy.detail: Paranodal loops anchor the myelin sheath beside each node and help segregate nodal sodium channels from juxtaparanodal potassium channels. This molecular organisation preserves efficient saltatory conduction.
anatomy.clinical: Disruption of paranodal proteins can impair conduction even before gross myelin loss is obvious.

anatomy.label: Axonal metabolic support
anatomy.detail: Oligodendrocytes transfer metabolic substrates, including lactate-related energy support, to axons. This is especially important for long, active axons with limited access to extracellular nutrients beneath compact myelin.
anatomy.clinical: Axonal degeneration in white-matter disease can reflect loss of trophic and metabolic support as well as loss of insulation.

quizBank.question: Why does myelin increase conduction speed?
options: It increases membrane resistance and decreases capacitance across internodes
It releases neurotransmitter along the entire axon
It removes all sodium channels from the axon
It converts electrical signals into hormones
quizBank.explanation: Myelin limits current leak and reduces the charge needed to change membrane voltage, allowing depolarising current to spread rapidly between nodes.

quizBank.question: What is distinctive about a central nervous system oligodendrocyte?
options: One cell can myelinate segments of several axons
It myelinates only one complete peripheral axon
It generates action potentials for nearby neurons
quizBank.explanation: A single oligodendrocyte extends multiple processes and forms separate internodes on several central nervous system axons.

quizBank.question: Where is an action potential regenerated during saltatory conduction?
quizBank.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels are densely concentrated at nodes of Ranvier, where the action potential is regenerated.

quizBank.question: Which statement best describes oligodendrocyte support of axons?
options: They provide both myelin and metabolic support
They provide insulation but no biological support
They form the blood-brain barrier alone
quizBank.explanation: Oligodendrocytes support axons electrically through myelin and metabolically through trophic and energy-related support.

quizBank.question: Why can white-matter disruption affect cognition broadly?
options: It can disturb timing and coordination across distributed networks
White matter stores all semantic memories
It selectively suppresses one emotion centre
It affects cognition only when the frontal lobe is destroyed
quizBank.explanation: Many cognitive operations depend on precisely timed communication across distant regions, making conduction efficiency clinically important.

sections.explainSimply: When a measured brain pattern meets a target, the system delivers a reward such as clearer video or points.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The reinforcement is contingent on a physiological feature rather than an overt action, although posture, gaze and muscle activity can accidentally control the reward if artifacts are not managed.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Effective shaping requires a genuine contingency, an achievable criterion and feedback close enough in time to the event being reinforced. Sham and yoked-feedback controls test whether specific contingency matters.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A driving instructor who gives immediate dashboard feedback while the learner practises a controllable skill.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand operant conditioning to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Rewarding artifact can produce impressive scores without meaningful neural learning.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using operant conditioning predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Rewarding artifact can produce impressive scores without meaningful neural learning. Evidence classification: established behavioural principle.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the central mechanism in this concept?
reviewPrompts.answer: Research describes heterogeneous alterations in frontolimbic reactivity, connectivity and learning across diagnostic groups, with substantial overlap with trauma exposure, mood disorders, neurodevelopmental conditions and substance use. Developmental models emphasise gene–environment interplay, attachment learning, reinforcement history, social cognition and state-dependent network dynamics. Group-level neural differences are not sufficiently specific for individual diagnosis.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the most important clinical caution?
reviewPrompts.answer: Biology may help explain vulnerability; it never excuses harm or makes change impossible. Formulate functions and learning histories, not “bad brain regions.”

reviewPrompts.prompt: What alternative explanations or red flags must be considered?
reviewPrompts.answer: Rigid threat predictions, unstable self-representation, impulsive reinforcement learning, interpersonal hypersensitivity or reduced behavioural flexibility can perpetuate crises and relational disruption. Similar patterns may reflect trauma, autism, ADHD, mood states, psychosis, substance effects or environmental danger and require careful differential assessment.
