pituitary-and-sella-atlas.title: Pituitary Gland & Sella Turcica Atlas
pituitary-and-sella-atlas.subtitle: Explore pituitary compartments, sellar relationships and hypothalamic control
pituitary-and-sella-atlas.altText: Chalkboard-style midsagittal and coronal views of the pituitary gland within the sella turcica, labelled with the optic chiasm, cavernous sinuses, sphenoid sinus, hypothalamus and infundibulum.
learningObjectives: Locate the pituitary gland within the sella turcica and identify its relationships to the optic chiasm, cavernous sinuses and sphenoid sinus.
Differentiate anterior and posterior pituitary organisation, inputs and outputs.
Relate sellar expansion and pituitary dysfunction to plausible visual, endocrine, neurological and psychological presentations without over-localising symptoms.

sections.explainSimply: The pituitary is a pea-sized hormone gland in a bony pocket beneath the brain. It receives instructions from the hypothalamus and helps regulate growth, stress, reproduction, thyroid function, water balance and lactation.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The pituitary is a major endocrine interface between brain and body. Changes in pituitary or hypothalamic function can alter energy, sleep, mood, cognition, sexual function, appetite and stress physiology, but these symptoms are nonspecific and require medical assessment.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The hypophysis sits in the hypophyseal fossa of the sphenoid bone. The anterior lobe receives hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting factors through the superior hypophyseal portal circulation; the posterior lobe contains axon terminals from supraoptic and paraventricular hypothalamic neurons. Superiorly lie the diaphragma sellae, infundibulum and optic chiasm; laterally are the cavernous sinuses containing the internal carotid arteries and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI; inferiorly lies the sphenoid sinus. Sellar and parasellar lesions may therefore combine endocrine, visual-field, ocular-motor, facial sensory and headache presentations.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of the hypothalamus as the executive office and the pituitary as the dispatch centre. The sella is the reinforced control booth, but nearby visual and cranial-nerve cables make expansion clinically important.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Pituitary disease can mimic or amplify depression, anxiety, fatigue, cognitive slowing, irritability, sleep disturbance and changes in motivation. Psychologists should recognise red flags and avoid assuming that endocrine-linked symptoms are purely psychological.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Pituitary hormone excess or deficiency can produce broad systemic and neuropsychiatric effects. Expanding masses may compress the optic chiasm, invade the cavernous sinus or disturb hypothalamic pathways. Symptom patterns vary with hormone type, lesion size, growth direction, treatment and comorbidity.
sections.clinicalPearl: A combination of new visual-field change, persistent headache and endocrine symptoms is a sellar-region red flag, not a personality formulation.
sections.clinicalExample: A person with fatigue, reduced libido, headaches and difficulty noticing objects at the outer edges of vision may require urgent medical and visual-field assessment for a sellar or suprasellar process; no single symptom proves pituitary disease.
sections.limitationsCautions: Hormonal symptoms are often gradual and nonspecific. Imaging size does not map neatly onto symptom severity, incidental pituitary lesions are common, and psychiatric presentations should not be attributed to pituitary dysfunction without endocrine and medical evidence.
sections.practicalExample: Use the relationship view to predict whether a lesion expanding superiorly, laterally or inferiorly would be more likely to affect vision, cavernous-sinus structures or the sphenoid sinus.

anatomy.position: Midline in the hypophyseal fossa of the sphenoid bone, inferior to the hypothalamus and optic chiasm, between the cavernous sinuses and superior to the sphenoid sinus.
spatialRelationships: Optic chiasm usually superior and slightly anterior
inputs: Hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones via portal vessels
Magnocellular axons from supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei
outputs: Vasopressin and oxytocin released from posterior pituitary terminals
connections: Posterior pituitary water-balance and reproductive pathways
bloodSupply: Superior hypophyseal arteries, usually from internal carotid and posterior communicating branches
Inferior hypophyseal arteries from cavernous internal carotid branches
Portal venous plexus linking median eminence to anterior pituitary
lesionPatterns: Bitemporal visual-field loss from chiasmal compression
Ocular-motor or trigeminal symptoms with cavernous-sinus extension
Diabetes insipidus with stalk or posterior-system involvement
Nonspecific fatigue, mood or cognitive change requiring endocrine correlation
associatedPresentations: Changes in growth, weight or body composition

stages.label: Hypothalamus
stages.text: Hypothalamic neurons detect internal state and generate releasing, inhibiting or neurosecretory signals.

stages.label: Pituitary route
stages.text: Signals travel through portal blood to the anterior lobe or down axons to the posterior lobe.

stages.label: Target organs
stages.text: Pituitary hormones influence thyroid, adrenal, gonadal, growth, lactation and water-balance systems.

stages.label: Feedback
stages.text: Peripheral hormones and physiological state feed back to hypothalamic and pituitary systems.

explorerParts.label: Anterior pituitary
explorerParts.detail: The adenohypophysis synthesises and releases ACTH, TSH, GH, prolactin, LH and FSH under hypothalamic and peripheral feedback control.
explorerParts.clinical: Functional adenomas may produce hormone excess; compression or treatment can reduce multiple axes.

explorerParts.label: Posterior pituitary
explorerParts.detail: The neurohypophysis stores and releases vasopressin and oxytocin made in hypothalamic magnocellular neurons.
explorerParts.clinical: Stalk or posterior-system injury can disturb water balance; diabetes insipidus is not expected from most isolated anterior adenomas.

explorerParts.label: Optic chiasm
explorerParts.detail: Crossing nasal retinal fibres lie close to the superior sellar region, although exact chiasmal position varies.
explorerParts.clinical: Superior expansion can cause classically bitemporal field loss, but visual patterns depend on anatomy and compression geometry.

explorerParts.label: Cavernous sinuses
explorerParts.detail: Each cavernous sinus contains the internal carotid artery and is related to cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI.
explorerParts.clinical: Lateral extension may cause diplopia, ophthalmoplegia or facial sensory symptoms; these require urgent medical evaluation.

explorerParts.label: Sphenoid sinus
explorerParts.detail: The sphenoid sinus lies inferior to the sellar floor and provides the common transsphenoidal surgical route.
explorerParts.clinical: Its anatomy matters for surgery and explains why inferior relationships differ from superior chiasmal effects.

polyvagal-theory.title: Polyvagal Theory
polyvagal-theory.subtitle: A clinically influential framework whose core neuroanatomical and evolutionary premises are actively disputed

learningObjectives: Explain polyvagal theory in clinically accurate language.

sections.explainSimply: Polyvagal Theory offers a state-based language for social engagement, mobilisation and shutdown, but that language should not be mistaken for settled autonomic neuroanatomy.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Some clinicians find its metaphors useful for discussing safety and state shifts. However, major claims about vagal hierarchy, vagal nuclei, vertebrate evolution and respiratory sinus arrhythmia are disputed in contemporary autonomic science, and the theory’s originator contests those critiques.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: If used clinically, treat Polyvagal Theory as a formulation heuristic rather than established neuroanatomy. Do not equate respiratory sinus arrhythmia with a direct readout of global “vagal tone,” infer a person’s putative ventral/dorsal vagal state from behaviour, or present the proposed evolutionary hierarchy as settled fact.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of polyvagal theory as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need polyvagal theory to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not diagnose “vagal states,” equate respiratory sinus arrhythmia with a direct measure of global vagal tone, or present the proposed vagal hierarchy as established anatomy.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use polyvagal theory to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses polyvagal theory to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Clinical metaphors may be useful without validating the theory’s disputed biological premises. Evidence classification: clinically influential, scientifically contested framework.

learningObjectives: Define processing speed without equating it with intelligence.

mechanismMap.label: Core function
mechanismMap.detail: Processing speed is how quickly the brain can take in simple information, make a small decision and respond accurately. It is not the same as intelligence or rushing.

mechanismMap.label: Neural systems
mechanismMap.detail: Speeded performance depends on distributed network integrity, myelination, white-matter connectivity, sensory encoding, motor output and strategic trade-offs between speed and accuracy. Processing speed is often a foundational constraint: when basic operations consume more time, working memory and executive resources become overloaded during complex tasks.

mechanismMap.label: Assessment pattern
mechanismMap.detail: Processing-speed measures sample visual scanning, graphomotor output, decision speed and sustained efficiency. Slow scores can reflect motor limitations, visual difficulty, fatigue, depression, medication effects, cautious style or broader white-matter inefficiency.

mechanismMap.label: Clinical translation
mechanismMap.detail: Psychologists should interpret speed scores alongside accuracy, motor demands, visual load and untimed reasoning. Slow speed can create real functional impairment even when reasoning is strong.

options: Fever, marked rigidity and altered consciousness after antipsychotic exposure

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the core clinical distinction?
reviewPrompts.answer: Medication response is evidence about treatment effect, not proof of a diagnosis or a single underlying chemical defect.

Simple “chemical imbalance” explanations are misleading. Drug effects are network-level, state-dependent and probabilistic. Pharmacokinetics determines absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination; pharmacodynamics concerns what the drug does at its targets. CYP interactions, half-life, active metabolites, withdrawal, adherence and placebo/nocebo processes all matter clinically. Psychological practice should support informed decision-making without prescribing outside scope.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What red flags or alternatives matter?
reviewPrompts.answer: New suicidality, severe agitation, serotonin-toxicity signs, manic activation, rigidity with fever, seizures or significant metabolic change require urgent medical review. Abrupt cessation can cause withdrawal or relapse.

sections.explainSimply: Rewards that are too rare frustrate learning; rewards that are too frequent provide little information.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Thresholds are commonly adjusted to maintain engagement while preserving contingency. Fixed, adaptive and percentile-based rules each alter the learning environment.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Schedule design should be prespecified where possible. Automatic thresholding may stabilise reward rate but can obscure whether the underlying signal changed.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A driving instructor who gives immediate dashboard feedback while the learner practises a controllable skill.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand reinforcement schedules to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not confuse a stable reward rate with successful training.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using reinforcement schedules predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not confuse a stable reward rate with successful training. Evidence classification: established behavioural principle; implementation-dependent.

learningObjectives: Explain why the neuronal interior is negative relative to the exterior at rest.
Distinguish the roles of leak channels, concentration gradients and Na+/K+-ATPase.

anatomy.label: Ion gradients
anatomy.detail: Sodium is concentrated outside the neuron and potassium inside. These gradients store potential energy across the membrane.
anatomy.clinical: Rapid changes in serum sodium or potassium can alter excitability and produce confusion, weakness or seizures.

anatomy.label: Potassium leak channels
anatomy.detail: At rest, potassium leak channels allow more potassium movement than sodium movement, pulling voltage toward the potassium equilibrium potential.
anatomy.clinical: Channel expression helps set how responsive a neuron is to incoming signals.

anatomy.label: Na+/K+-ATPase
anatomy.detail: The pump uses ATP to move three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in, preserving gradients over time.
anatomy.clinical: Hypoxia and metabolic failure compromise the pump, causing ionic collapse and cellular swelling.

anatomy.label: Intracellular anions
anatomy.detail: Large negatively charged proteins and phosphates remain trapped inside the cell and contribute to intracellular negativity.
anatomy.clinical: Cell injury can disturb osmotic and ionic balance even without a primary channel disorder.

stages.label: Separate
stages.text: ATP-dependent transport maintains sodium outside and potassium inside.

stages.label: Leak
stages.text: Potassium moves down its concentration gradient through leak channels.

options: Maintain sodium and potassium gradients over time
quizBank.explanation: The pump preserves the concentration gradients that support membrane voltage.

quizBank.question: Why is the inside of a resting neuron relatively negative?
options: Selective ion permeability and retained intracellular anions
Because electrons flow down the axon
Because all sodium leaves the cell
Because the nucleus is negatively charged
quizBank.explanation: Selective permeability and fixed intracellular anions produce relative intracellular negativity.

quizBank.question: What usually happens if extracellular potassium rises substantially?
options: The resting voltage becomes less negative
quizBank.explanation: A reduced potassium gradient tends to depolarise the membrane and alter excitability.

quizBank.question: “Resting” membrane potential means the neuron is:
options: Not firing an action potential but still metabolically active
quizBank.explanation: Resting neurons actively maintain gradients and receive continuous input.

reticular-activating-system-atlas.subtitle: Map ascending arousal pathways from brainstem to thalamus and cortex

learningObjectives: Identify the major components of the reticular activating system atlas.

sections.explainSimply: The reticular activating system helps keep the brain awake, alert and responsive.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Arousal depends on distributed brainstem, hypothalamic, basal forebrain, thalamic and cortical systems rather than one switch.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Ascending neuromodulatory nuclei include noradrenergic locus coeruleus, serotonergic raphe, cholinergic pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei, dopaminergic midbrain systems and histaminergic tuberomammillary pathways. These converge through thalamic and extrathalamic routes to regulate cortical state.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A building-wide power and alertness network with several backup generators, not a single light switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Damage can produce reduced consciousness, fluctuating attention, sleep-wake disruption or impaired state regulation; diffuse metabolic and pharmacological effects can mimic focal disruption.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Damage or dysregulation can disrupt arousal, sleep-wake regulation, attention readiness; presentations depend on laterality, extent and connected networks.
sections.clinicalPearl: Always separate arousal level from cognitive content: a person cannot demonstrate cognition reliably when state regulation is unstable.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses the reticular activating system atlas map to test whether a patient’s pattern is anatomically coherent while considering broader network and medical explanations.
sections.limitationsCautions: Atlas localisation supports hypothesis generation, not diagnosis. Individual anatomy, distributed processing, compensation and comorbidity limit one-to-one structure–symptom claims.

anatomy.position: Integrated within deep or medial cortical-brainstem relationships shown in the atlas.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the reticular activating system atlas?
options: Arousal depends on distributed brainstem, hypothalamic, basal forebrain, thalamic and cortical systems rather than one switch.
It acts independently of the rest of the brain.
It has one fixed psychological function.
It can diagnose psychiatric disorders from anatomy alone.
quiz.rationale: The structure participates in distributed networks and should be interpreted in context.

quiz.question: What is the safest clinical inference from this atlas?
options: A lesion pattern can guide hypotheses but requires clinical and medical correlation.
One symptom proves one structure is damaged.
quiz.rationale: Neuroanatomy constrains hypotheses but does not replace assessment.

quiz.question: Why are connections important?
options: Symptoms can reflect disconnection and downstream network effects.
All pathways are identical across people.
quiz.rationale: Distributed cognitive systems depend on pathways linking regions.

sections.thinkOfItLike: A rehabilitation plan: define the target, dose, measurement and stopping rule before changing the exercise.

sections.whenItGoesWrong: “More” is not always better; excessive activation may worsen symptoms.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using reward bands predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: “More” is not always better; excessive activation may worsen symptoms. Evidence classification: protocol-specific; evidence varies.

sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses salience network changes to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not treat connectivity maps as direct readouts of symptoms. Evidence classification: promising network evidence.

anatomy.clinical: Medication and neurological disease can disrupt state control.

anatomy.clinical: Fragmentation may reduce restorative and memory-related processes.

quizBank.explanation: OSA involves recurrent upper-airway obstruction, oxygen fluctuation and arousal.

options: Increase arousal and strengthen wakefulness in bed

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the central mechanism in this concept?
reviewPrompts.answer: Sleep–wake regulation emerges from interaction between circadian signals from the suprachiasmatic nucleus, homeostatic sleep pressure, hypothalamic sleep-promoting neurons, ascending arousal systems and orexin-mediated state stability. Disorder mechanisms differ: hyperarousal and learned associations in insomnia; upper-airway obstruction and autonomic surges in OSA; phase misalignment in circadian disorders; REM/NREM state dissociation in parasomnias.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the most important clinical caution?
reviewPrompts.answer: “I sleep badly” is a symptom, not a mechanism. Separate insomnia, circadian misalignment, breathing disturbance, movement and hypersomnolence before choosing treatment.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What alternative explanations or red flags must be considered?
reviewPrompts.answer: Chronic insomnia can perpetuate distress and functional impairment; untreated OSA increases cardiovascular and cognitive risk; severe sleep deprivation may worsen mania, psychosis, seizures and suicidality. Red flags include dangerous sleepiness, nocturnal breathing pauses, cataplexy or injurious parasomnias.

subcortex.title: Below the Cortex
subcortex.subtitle: Subcortical systems shape the whole brain
learningObjectives: Identify major subcortical systems relevant to cognition, affect, movement and homeostasis.
Explain cortico-subcortical loops rather than treating deep nuclei as isolated modules.
Relate subcortical dysfunction to cognitive, behavioural and autonomic presentations.

sections.explainSimply: Important structures sit deep inside the brain. They help control movement, memory, emotion, motivation and body regulation.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The thalamus coordinates information flow; basal ganglia support action selection and habit; hippocampal systems support memory; hypothalamus regulates homeostasis; amygdala contributes to salience and threat learning.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops and limbic circuits integrate cognition, affect, motor control and reinforcement. Subcortical structures are heterogeneous nuclei, not unitary emotion modules.
sections.thinkOfItLike: The city’s transport hub, security network, archive and utilities department operating beneath the visible skyline.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Subcortical dysfunction can mimic “purely psychological” problems through apathy, impulsivity, memory change, sleep disruption or altered emotional learning.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Degeneration, hypoxia, inflammation and focal injury may disrupt movement, memory, motivation or autonomic regulation.
sections.clinicalPearl: Deep structures influence cortical processing continuously; “higher” does not mean independent.
sections.practicalExample: Disruption of frontostriatal circuits can produce slowed initiation, reduced cognitive flexibility or apathy even when primary cortical sensory and motor systems remain relatively intact.
sections.limitationsCautions: Terms such as “limbic system” and “basal ganglia” group heterogeneous structures. Clinical reasoning should specify nuclei, pathways and network context where possible.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the central mechanism in this concept?
reviewPrompts.answer: Drugs differ pharmacologically but can converge on mesocorticolimbic dopamine and downstream plasticity. Incentive sensitisation may amplify cue-triggered wanting; allostatic adaptation shifts hedonic set points; dorsal striatal recruitment supports habitual responding; prefrontal and interoceptive networks influence choice and relapse. These models are complementary, not universal explanations for every person.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the most important clinical caution?
reviewPrompts.answer: Dopamine is not simply pleasure. It helps update motivational significance and learning. Addiction is neither pure choice nor loss of all agency—it is constrained, learned behaviour that can change with effective support.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What alternative explanations or red flags must be considered?
reviewPrompts.answer: Tolerance, withdrawal, overdose, seizures, psychosis, mood destabilisation, cognitive impairment and interpersonal harm vary by substance and pattern. Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal can be medically dangerous; opioid overdose can suppress breathing.

learningObjectives: Describe presynaptic release, cleft diffusion and postsynaptic receptor activation.

anatomy.label: Presynaptic terminal
anatomy.detail: The terminal contains vesicles, active zones and voltage-gated calcium channels that couple an arriving spike to transmitter release.
anatomy.clinical: Botulinum toxin and several disease processes alter vesicle-release machinery.

anatomy.label: Calcium channels
anatomy.detail: Depolarisation opens presynaptic calcium channels. Local calcium concentration rises sharply and activates proteins that drive vesicle fusion.
anatomy.clinical: Small changes in calcium entry can substantially change release probability.

anatomy.label: Synaptic cleft
anatomy.detail: Released transmitter diffuses across a narrow extracellular space before reaching receptors.
anatomy.clinical: Diffusion is rapid, but transmitter clearance is essential to preserve timing and specificity.

anatomy.label: Postsynaptic receptors
anatomy.detail: Ionotropic receptors directly gate channels; metabotropic receptors activate slower intracellular signalling cascades.
anatomy.clinical: The same transmitter can produce different effects through different receptor subtypes.

anatomy.label: Clearance systems
anatomy.detail: Transporters, enzymes and diffusion remove transmitter from the cleft and recycle components.
anatomy.clinical: Transporter blockade is a major mechanism of antidepressants and stimulants.

sections.explainSimply: The thalamus is a paired hub deep in the brain. Most sensory information, and many motor and attention signals, pass through specialised thalamic nuclei before reaching cortex.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The thalamus is not a passive relay. Its nuclei gate information according to state, salience and cortical feedback, contributing to attention, arousal, memory and the coordination of distributed cognitive networks.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Each thalamus borders the third ventricle and is divided by internal medullary laminae into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups. Ventral posterior nuclei relay somatosensation; geniculate bodies relay visual and auditory information; ventral anterior and lateral nuclei participate in basal ganglia and cerebellar motor loops; anterior and mediodorsal nuclei support limbic and prefrontal functions; pulvinar and intralaminar nuclei contribute to association, attention and arousal. Clinical effects depend on laterality, vascular territory and network disconnection.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of a secure rail interchange: different platforms serve different destinations, while cortical feedback continually changes which trains are prioritised.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Thalamic injury can alter attention, memory, language, arousal, affect and sensory experience. Recognising a distributed thalamocortical pattern helps avoid mislabelling neurological changes as purely psychiatric.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A focal thalamic lesion may cause hemisensory loss, central pain, memory impairment, language or neglect-like symptoms, reduced alertness or executive change. Symptoms rarely identify a single nucleus without imaging and neurological examination.
sections.clinicalPearl: Bilateral paramedian thalamic injury can produce profound arousal and memory disturbance because it disrupts midline nuclei and their widespread cortical connections.
sections.clinicalExample: A person with a left paramedian thalamic infarct may present with fluctuating alertness, slowed initiation and memory difficulty despite relatively preserved primary strength.
sections.limitationsCautions: Atlas localisation supports hypothesis generation, not diagnosis. Thalamic nuclei are small, boundaries vary across atlases, and behavioural outcomes reflect connected cortical and subcortical systems.
sections.practicalExample: Use the thalamus atlas map to test whether a clinical pattern is anatomically coherent while considering network and medical alternatives.

quizBank.question: A premonitory urge is:
options: An uncomfortable sensation that may precede a tic
quizBank.explanation: Many people experience an urge or tension relieved briefly by the tic.

quizBank.question: The most relevant circuit model involves:
quizBank.explanation: Action selection and inhibition loops are central to current models.

quizBank.question: Evidence-based behavioural treatment for tics includes:
options: CBIT with awareness and competing responses
quizBank.explanation: CBIT targets tic management without moralising or coercive suppression.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the central mechanism in this concept?
reviewPrompts.answer: Models emphasise altered basal-ganglia inhibition, sensorimotor prediction, habit learning and heightened salience of premonitory urges. Dopaminergic modulation is relevant but insufficient as a complete explanation. Voluntary control and involuntary generation coexist: a person may consciously release a tic to relieve an involuntary urge. Comorbid ADHD, OCD and anxiety often contribute more impairment than tic frequency alone.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the most important clinical caution?
reviewPrompts.answer: Suppressibility does not make a tic voluntary in the ordinary sense; effortful control can coexist with involuntary urge generation.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What alternative explanations or red flags must be considered?
reviewPrompts.answer: Sudden explosive onset of complex tic-like behaviour, especially with marked social modelling or atypical phenomenology, requires careful differential assessment. New neurological signs or medication-related onset need medical review.

quizBank.question: Diffuse axonal injury primarily involves:
options: Stretching and disruption of long white-matter axons
quizBank.explanation: Rotational and acceleration forces can disrupt axons across distributed pathways.

quizBank.question: After uncomplicated mild TBI, best-practice recovery usually includes:
options: Brief relative rest followed by graded return to activity
Weeks of complete sensory isolation for everyone
Avoiding all movement until every symptom disappears
Routine structural imaging as the sole guide
quizBank.explanation: Prolonged strict rest may worsen deconditioning and symptom focus; graded activity is generally preferred.

quizBank.question: Which feature requires urgent medical assessment?
quizBank.explanation: Neurological deterioration after head injury may indicate intracranial complication.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the central mechanism in this concept?
reviewPrompts.answer: Primary injury includes focal contusion, haemorrhage, axonal stretch and vascular disruption. Secondary cascades involve excitotoxicity, ionic imbalance, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation and altered cerebral metabolism. Diffuse axonal injury preferentially affects long white-matter pathways and can produce disconnection without a large focal lesion. Persistent symptoms after mild TBI are multifactorial and may be maintained by sleep disturbance, pain, vestibular dysfunction, threat appraisal, mood and deconditioning.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What is the most important clinical caution?
reviewPrompts.answer: Symptoms after mild TBI are real, but persistent difficulty is rarely explained by one damaged brain region. Recovery is biological, cognitive and contextual.

reviewPrompts.prompt: What alternative explanations or red flags must be considered?
reviewPrompts.answer: Red flags include deteriorating consciousness, repeated vomiting, seizure, focal weakness, worsening severe headache, unequal pupils or new confusion. Repeated injuries can increase risk and warrant careful return-to-play or work decisions.

ventricular-system-atlas.title: Ventricular System Atlas
ventricular-system-atlas.subtitle: Trace CSF flow through ventricles, foramina and subarachnoid spaces
ventricular-system-atlas.altText: Chalkboard-style interactive anatomical illustration for Ventricular System Atlas, showing labelled structures and pathway relationships.
learningObjectives: Identify the major components of ventricular system.
Trace clinically relevant inputs, outputs and connections.
Relate focal dysfunction to plausible neurological and behavioural signs.

sections.explainSimply: Ventricular System is a set of connected structures that can be explored layer by layer to understand where it sits and what it does.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: This atlas links the anatomy of ventricular system to behaviour, cognition, neurological signs and clinically meaningful patterns without reducing complex functions to one structure.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The ventricular system should be interpreted through spatial relationships, laterality, vascular supply, pathway continuity and distributed network effects. Focal damage can create both local signs and disconnection syndromes.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of it as a layered transit map: structures are stations, tracts are routes, and symptoms depend on which junctions or connections are interrupted.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Recognising plausible neuroanatomical patterns supports better referral, formulation and interpretation of cognitive or behavioural change.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Over-localising a symptom to one structure, or treating an atlas view as diagnostic evidence, can produce false certainty.
sections.clinicalPearl: Their shape follows the expanding cerebral hemispheres.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician can select a structure in the Ventricular System Atlas and trace its inputs and outputs before comparing the predicted pattern with examination, imaging and functional assessment.
sections.limitationsCautions: This atlas supports learning and clinical reasoning; it does not replace neurological examination, imaging or specialist interpretation.

anatomy.label: Lateral ventricles
anatomy.function: Paired C-shaped chambers within cerebral hemispheres
anatomy.inputs: Choroid plexus and CSF from ventricular lining
anatomy.connections: Choroid plexus and CSF from ventricular lining; projects to Interventricular foramina to third ventricle.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Their shape follows the expanding cerebral hemispheres.

anatomy.label: Third ventricle
anatomy.function: Midline chamber between thalami
anatomy.inputs: Lateral ventricles via foramina of Monro
anatomy.connections: Lateral ventricles via foramina of Monro; projects to Cerebral aqueduct.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: A narrow midline chamber tightly related to diencephalic structures.

anatomy.label: Cerebral aqueduct
anatomy.function: Narrow conduit through midbrain
anatomy.connections: Third ventricle; projects to Fourth ventricle.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Its small calibre makes it a common bottleneck for CSF flow.

anatomy.label: Fourth ventricle
anatomy.function: Diamond-shaped chamber between pons/medulla and cerebellum
anatomy.connections: Cerebral aqueduct; projects to Median and lateral apertures.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: It opens CSF into the subarachnoid space.

mechanismMap.label: Core function
mechanismMap.detail: Visuospatial skills help you understand shapes, distance, direction and how pieces fit together. They are different from eyesight itself.

mechanismMap.label: Neural systems
mechanismMap.detail: Right-lateralised parietal and occipitoparietal networks are prominent in spatial attention and construction, but performance is distributed and task-dependent. Errors may reflect neglect, simultanagnosia, apraxia, executive disorganisation, motor limitations or primary visual impairment. Qualitative error analysis is essential.

mechanismMap.label: Assessment pattern
mechanismMap.detail: Visuospatial performance draws on visual perception, spatial attention, construction, mental rotation and integration of parts into wholes. Dorsal-stream systems emphasise spatial action and location; ventral-stream systems emphasise object identity.

mechanismMap.label: Clinical translation
mechanismMap.detail: Psychologists must distinguish perceptual, attentional, motor and executive causes of poor construction. The same low score can arise from very different mechanisms and require different supports.

mechanismMap.label: Core concept
mechanismMap.detail: Electrical fields spread through cerebrospinal fluid, skull and skin before reaching electrodes. Each sensor therefore samples a mixture of sources.

mechanismMap.label: Mechanism
mechanismMap.detail: Volume conduction blurs spatial localisation and inflates zero-lag similarity between channels. Source modelling can reduce ambiguity but depends on modelling assumptions and signal quality.

mechanismMap.label: Clinical integration
mechanismMap.detail: This explains why topographic colour does not equal a sharply bounded cortical lesion and why connectivity metrics require caution.

mechanismMap.label: Boundary condition
mechanismMap.detail: Treating neighbouring electrodes as independent brain regions can exaggerate localisation and connectivity claims.

sections.explainSimply: The window of tolerance describes a zone where a person can remain engaged without becoming overwhelmed or shut down.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: It is useful for pacing and shared language, but it is not a measurable neural boundary.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Arousal capacity varies by task, relationship, sleep, pain and context; treatment should expand flexibility rather than enforce one “correct” state.

mechanismMap.label: Core function
mechanismMap.detail: Working memory is the brain’s mental workbench. It lets you hold a small amount of information in mind while doing something with it.

mechanismMap.label: Neural systems
mechanismMap.detail: Working memory depends on dynamic frontoparietal coordination rather than a single storage site. Prefrontal systems support goal maintenance and interference control, while posterior regions represent domain-specific content. Capacity reflects both representational fidelity and the ability to protect task-relevant information from interference.

mechanismMap.label: Assessment pattern
mechanismMap.detail: Working memory includes temporary maintenance and active manipulation. Verbal and visuospatial stores interact with attentional control and long-term knowledge. Performance is limited and vulnerable to distraction, stress, fatigue and excessive task complexity.

mechanismMap.label: Clinical translation
mechanismMap.detail: Working-memory weaknesses affect multistep instructions, mental arithmetic, reading comprehension and self-regulation. External supports reduce load and often improve real-world functioning more than repeated “brain training.”

sections.explainSimply: Holding a distressing image in mind while doing another demanding task can tax limited working-memory resources.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Competition may make the recalled image temporarily less vivid and emotional, enabling new appraisal or updating.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Dual-task studies support the prediction that taxing working memory during recall can reduce the vividness and emotionality of remembered material. This supports a plausible component mechanism, but does not establish working-memory taxation as the complete explanation for clinical EMDR outcomes.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of working memory theory as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need working memory theory to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Reducing vividness is not the same as resolving meaning or risk.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use working memory theory to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses working memory theory to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Reducing vividness or emotionality in a dual-task paradigm is not the same as resolving trauma meaning, functional impairment or risk. Evidence classification: experimentally supported component mechanism; incomplete account of clinical EMDR efficacy.

sections.explainSimply: Z-score systems compare selected EEG features with a normative database and may reward movement toward the reference range.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: A z-score describes statistical distance under specific acquisition and processing assumptions; it does not diagnose or define an optimal state.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Multivariate and “live” z-score systems can train many features simultaneously, complicating contingency, causal interpretation and replication.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Choosing a camera lens: every method emphasises some information and introduces its own distortions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand z-score neurofeedback to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Normalising numbers is not the same as improving the person.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using z-score neurofeedback predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Normalising numbers is not the same as improving the person. Evidence classification: emerging; mixed and limited controlled evidence.

Z-score systems compare selected EEG features with a normative database and may reward movement toward the reference range.
A z-score describes statistical distance under specific acquisition and processing assumptions; it does not diagnose or define an optimal state.
Normalising numbers is not the same as improving the person.

quizBank.question: How should the evidence for Z-Score Neurofeedback be communicated?
